The path

σπήλαιον

The Cave

spḗlaion

In Athena’s teaching

For her the Allegory of the Cave holds the whole teaching of awakening in one image, and Plato gives it as his answer to what paideia is. She reads the cave as a tomb and also as a womb: leaving it is a birth, with conception, gestation, labour and a midwife. In her reading the prisoners are chained by legs and neck but their hands are free, meaning free will and the heart can never be enslaved. The root cave is not society or even the body but the way an unknowing mind binds itself, and the freed must go back down out of love and justice.

Another angle

The Cave is her favourite allegory because it condenses the whole path of liberation, and Socrates gives it as the definition of παιδεία. She reads every detail as a symbol: bound legs mean no movement and so no life, the bound neck a blocked link between mind and heart, the free hands free will. The cave is also the brain, its fire the inner cinema of vision, and it is both womb and tomb, so leaving it is death and second birth. Its exit is not a place: 'you are the gate', and the freed one must return to see the One in every form.

Another angle

For her the Cave (Republic VII, 514a, third after the Sun and the Divided Line) holds the whole Hellenic path of awakening: if all else were lost, we would still have the path. Its forgotten ending is the key: the freed one must go back down, out of compassion, to understand, celebrate and raise the sensible world to its highest beauty, so the cave is a place to transfigure, not a prison to flee. She reads it on three levels (political, inner, mystical); finally the cave is a function of consciousness.

Athena connects it to

  • Paideia

    Plato offers the allegory when asked to define paideia.

  • Second birth of the soul

    The cave is a womb and its exit the gate of the soul's birth.

  • Free will

    The free hands of the prisoners stand for free will.

  • Lethe, forgetting

    The chains are forgetting; the prisoners sleep in the cosmic dream.

  • The sudden

    Release from the chains comes 'suddenly'.

  • Immanence

    The freed must return into the cave to complete initiation.

  • The Sun

    Outside, the freed one sees reflections first, then the sun itself.

  • Turning of the soul

    The first liberating act is the prisoner turning around.

The good life

παιδεία

Paideia

paideía

In Athena’s teaching

Paideia is not diplomas, rote learning (παπαγαλία) or technical training but the art of turning the whole eye of the soul from outside to inside, from becoming toward being and the Good. She ties the word to παῖς, the child: it is all for the child, the awakening of the sacred child, the eternal being one already is. In society it is the gate that joins the citizen to the polity, which is why every power has wanted to control it. She reads modern Greek resignation partly as the result of paideia being stripped away.

Another angle

The Cave is Plato's answer to the question 'what is paideia?', and the Sun simile shows its method: as the sun activates sight already in the eye, education activates the knowledge already within, so do not stuff children with information. Paideia and politics are 'the two Ps', life's two gates, and changing paideia is the root way to change a constitution. The educator's first task is to light the light within and shine it on others.

Another angle

Παιδεία in her teaching is not the Ministry of Education's school system but spiritual education, a way of awakening and of εὐδαιμονία. Socrates defines it in the Republic as μεταστροφή, the turning of the soul from phenomena toward truth, light and being. In the Pythagoras lesson it has four stages, and in the 28 October talk it is the only soil in which a political change can take root.

The path

μεταστροφή

Turning of the soul

metastrophḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Μεταστροφή is the turn from looking outward to looking inward. You will never find the exit of the cave in the senses or in space and time, where you only bang on the wall and go deeper; you must turn all your attention within. She reads the pandemic as the world forcing this turn on everyone, and the 28 October talk opens by turning attention from a remembered past to the now. What usually sets it off is being fed up with the torment of change.

Another angle

Μεταστροφή, the turning around of the soul's eye, is for her Plato's definition of paideia (Republic 518d): the whole soul turns from phenomena and becoming toward being and the Good. Because the visible world is an inverted reflection in the mirror of becoming, the turn is a literal reversal of attention from outside to inside. She treats it as the practical heart of philosophy, and as the remedy that slowly dries the passions.

Another angle

Plato's definition of paideia in the cave allegory is μεταστροφή, the turning of the eye of the soul: where, how, what and why we look. Since the sun never sets and only we turn, awakening is a turn of vision rather than a change in the world. Consciousness, like a searchlight, lives whatever it is turned toward.

  • The Good

  • Pain as a wake-up call

  • The senses

    Turn the eyes of the soul, not the physical eyes

Cosmos and the One

πῦρ ἀείζωον

Ever-living fire

pŷr aeízōon

In Athena’s teaching

Reading Heraclitus B30, she holds that the whole cosmos, intelligible, psychic and material, is an ever-living fire that no god or human made, so maker and made are one. This fire is not candle flame or electricity, which are only its reflections in the cave, but Logos, primordial consciousness, which the Platonists call Nous. It is 'kindled in measures and quenched in measures' not like a radiator switched on and off but as manifesting and unmanifest at the same moment, like the frames of a film. In Part B she extends it: justice itself is the finest, fastest fire running through everything.

Another angle

Fire is the nature of the true self: she derives δαίμων partly from δαίω, 'to be aflame', so at your core you are a flame of pure truth, a fiery focal point (ἑστία). Hestia's ever-living fire meeting the river's water produces the soul's exhalation, and Heraclitus' wisest, dry soul raises its 'scent' to incandescence. She also derives αὔρα from a root meaning 'to kindle' (her etymology, flagged uncertain).

Another angle

Fire and light run through her etymologies: philo- as fire igniting the inner fire, φ in φιλία as light that envelops, σοφία as inner light, phenomena as flashes of light within the mind. The daimon comes from burning, a local flame of Heraclitus's ever-living fire, and being set on fire is a stated purpose of philosophy; the soul is that fire cooled. In Plato's image the Good is the Sun.

The good life

τὸ ἀγαθόν

The Good

tò agathón

In Athena’s teaching

The Good is the first sun, the μέγιστον μάθημα, without which no other learning counts as true knowledge. It is beyond knowledge and truth, so it is touched and lived rather than understood; its light is truth and its heat is eros. In her vocabulary the small word εὖ names this inner light: whatever is joined to it takes on goodness, and diving to one's core one finds that one's being is the Good. Following Plotinus she says that when you know it you recognise it as yourself, and it comes 'like one who never left'.

Another angle

In the Sun simile the Good is the sun of the intelligible: it emits the light of truth, activates the nous to see, and makes ideas intelligible. Like the sun, which is the source of light without being light, the Good is the source of truth and knowledge without being either: a spring is not water. It is unknowable, so awakening is uniting with it, not knowing it; after the return to the cave she says all is the Good, even darkness.

Another angle

The Good is the first principle and first cause, to which all causes trace back, and the sun outside the cave. She distinguishes it even from essence: οὐσία is unified pure consciousness without subject or object, while the Sun of the Good is the source, beyond consciousness. Yet the cave is not elsewhere: it is the Good's 'underground', differing by depth or vibration. Our entelechy is to attune our existence to it.

The good life

εὐδαιμονία

Eudaimonia

eudaimonía

In Athena’s teaching

Eudaimonia is the final cause of all causes: behind every car, marriage or job lies the wish for it, and nothing lies behind it (Aristotle). She defines it as an unshakeable fullness and freedom that depends on no condition, and as recognising your inner fiery δαίμων, which separates it from εὐτυχία, luck that turns with chance's wheel. Security, goods and relationships are conditions for cultivating it, never its source; it comes only from the soul's inward turning, and the awakened work for the εὐδαιμονία of all beings.

Another angle

Eudaimonia is a stable fullness that does not ride fortune's wheel: it holds 'come rain or snow' because it rests on our own nature, not on anything external. She sets it against εὐτυχία, good luck, which rises and falls with τύχη; her image is Odysseus tied to his mast. It is also political, since for Aristotle the lawgiver aims at the eudaimonia of the whole city. Recognising one's true nature as fire and as the Good is itself freedom and eudaimonia, which Pythagoras named 'the best'.

Another angle

Not good luck or passing happiness: εὖ is the divine pure nature, the Good, and δαίμων the inner spirit, so eudaimonia is the inner flame touching its own source. It is lasting, unwavering wholeness that arises only from self-knowledge and never from possessions or circumstances. With Aristotle she calls it the goal of all goals and the inner programme of human nature, and she faults modern education for leaving it out.

Roots

εὖ (the good, divine pure nature) + δαίμων (inner spirit, true self)

Happiness is the inner divine spark united with the Good. standard

Thinkers

Ἡράκλειτος

Heraclitus

Hērákleitos

In Athena’s teaching

People call him 'the dark', but she calls him the most luminous philosopher she has met, one you need a 'Delian diver' to reach. She builds whole talks on his fragments: B30 on the ever-living fire, B52 on Aion as a child playing, B118 on the dry soul, the common Logos (ξυνός), and Dionysus and Hades being the same. For her he teaches a radical non-dualism in which the poet and the poem are one.

Another angle

Heraclitus gives her the river of becoming ('everything flows') into which the soul is plunged, truth as flow rather than a fixed banner, and the dry soul as wisest. Above all she returns to his Aeon as a child playing dice: life as divine play, the dice as the One's possibilities that sensation helps bring into actuality. His 'all is one' answers where we could go to find the One.

Another angle

Heraclitus appears in every talk. His fragment 50, 'it is wise to agree that all things are one', is for her the first principle of Hellenism. His logos is one and common (κοινὸς λόγος) while sleepers think they own a private mind, and his ever-living fire is what the touch of truth kindles. In the Ares lesson she cites him on mortals and immortals living each other's death.

Thinkers

Πλάτων

Plato

Plátōn

In Athena’s teaching

Plato is her main source, read as an initiatory teacher of awakening rather than a builder of abstract systems. She treats the Republic, subtitled 'On the Just', as so complete that if it alone survived it would carry the quintessence of Hellenic philosophy, and its three similes (Sun, Line, Cave) as a staged map of ascent. She also draws on the Phaedo (philosophy as practice of dying), the Symposium (Diotima), the Theaetetus (maieutics), the Timaeus, the Phaedrus and above all the Cratylus for etymologies.

Another angle

Plato is the backbone of her teaching: the Republic (which she calls the Bible of Hellenism) and its Cave, the Timaeus on soul and sensation, the Symposium's Diotima. She rejects the dualist Plato who scorns the senses and reads him as a holistic teacher of awakening whose Academy taught philosophy as a path of freedom and science until Justinian's edict. Reading the Euthyphro at 14 felt to her like remembering, Plato's own ἀνάμνησις.

Another angle

Plato is her main text. The Republic gives the Cave, παιδεία as turning, the three parts of the soul and the city-soul mirroring; the Phaedo the practice of death and 'make music'; the Symposium Diotima; the Timaeus a Greek theory of the soul's seats in the body; the Cratylus her ἀρετή etymology. She adds his third category between being and non-being: becoming, the zone that 'is and is not' where the soul stirs and turns.

The good life

ἔρως

Eros

érōs

In Athena’s teaching

Eros, with wonder, is the beginning of philosophy and of all change: to love freedom, true life, the εὖ ζῆν. She derives it from ῥέω, to flow: a cosmic current that passes through you and makes you lose the old false self, which is exactly the point. In the Sun simile eros is the heat of the Good as truth is its light, so the real philosopher is incandescent rather than coldly detached, and the first trait Socrates asks of a philosopher-leader is to be ἐρωτικός. It cannot be engineered with 'five tips'; it is the mystery of the Good, and she separates it sharply from attachment and obsession.

Another angle

She links ἔρως to εἴρω, to join and fit together (also the root of εἰρήνη, peace), and to ἐρῶ, 'I say', so eros, logos and peace belong together. Cosmically eros is the weft of universal harmony, the glue that keeps the world and our true nature from perishing. It is the strongest power in the universe and a double-edged knife: its quality shapes our health, relationships, self-knowledge and even our society. Greek philosophy does not renounce it but asks us to know it from within and steer it with the divine nous toward its natural goal.

Another angle

Eros is not mere bodily attraction but the soul's impetus (ὁρμή) toward union, a rushing flow that carries us from loving one person to loving the city and the cosmos. Philosophy begins as Eros for truth, being passionately and ontologically in love with the Good. Even questioning is erotic in her reading: the eros of the question leads to the all of the answer.

Roots

ῥέω / ῥοή (to flow / flow)

Eros is a cosmic current flowing through you. Athena’s reading

The good life

εὖ ζῆν

Living well

eû zên

In Athena’s teaching

Starting from Alexander, who owed ζῆν to his parents and εὖ ζῆν to Aristotle, she defines living well as one's relationship with oneself, not success, money or fame. It means freedom, virtue, inner peace (γαλήνη, ἀταραξία) and care for the common good, and it is a feast to celebrate rather than a life to endure. Paradoxically she calls it the easy path: what is hard is being tossed up and down by every honk and setback. Collective εὖ ζῆν is also the purpose of justice and what the just leader serves.

Another angle

She opens by naming what she and the host share: love for εὐδαιμονία, for εὖ ζῆν, 'true life', and for the union of science and spirituality that fulfils it. This, she says, is both the meaning and the purpose of Greek philosophy as the ancients defined it.

    Paideia is the way to εὖ ζῆν.

    Collective εὖ ζῆν is the purpose of justice.

  • Philosophy

    Living well is philosophy's purpose.

  • Science and spirit

The good life

δικαιοσύνη / τὸ δίκαιον

Justice

dikaiosýnē / tò díkaion

In Athena’s teaching

Justice is not 'getting my rights' or punishment but balance held from the middle of Themis's scale, a collective state that brings things back to the mean. Inwardly it is τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν, each part of the soul doing its own around the one fiery Self, so it is an energy and a state rather than an act. Beyond the cave, in her reading of the Cratylus, justice is the finest, fastest fire passing through all things, the self-regulation of the cosmic fire that keeps the universe balanced. With eros it is one of the two keys to the Good, and it is why the freed must return to the cave.

Another angle

Far more than a political institution, justice for Plato and his successors is the virtue of virtues, the union of all virtues, or the state of awakening and pure beholding. It unites the divisible and the indivisible, finding the sacred mean of Heraclitus's 'one-all'. Geometrically it is the harmony of all levels, which is why she calls φ its magic key and ties the Line's five to five as the Pythagorean rhythm of justice.

Another angle

The Republic, as she presents it, starts from defining justice and ends by defining everything: soul, polis, afterlife, music and education. When asked to define justice, Socrates would first ask what use the definition has in life. Her chosen line from Plato makes justice the condition of wisdom: knowledge severed from justice and the other virtues is mere cunning.

Athena connects it to

    Justice is the subtlest fire pervading the cosmos.

  • Harmony

    Justice is balance and harmonisation of opposites.

  • The true Self

    Doing one's own means acting from the one fiery Self.

  • Immanence

    Justice requires the freed to return to the cave.

  • Respecting shame

    Shame is justice regulating itself within.

  • Eros

    Eros and the just are the two keys to the Good.

  • Plato

    The Republic is 'On the Just'.

  • Living well

    Its purpose is the collective εὖ ζῆν.

Soul and mind

νοῦς

Nous

noûs

In Athena’s teaching

In this talk she uses νοῦς as a near synonym of consciousness and says it can work in five ways, which together make up Plato's theory of knowledge. Her central claim is that there is one wonder-worker, one prisoner, one light and one awakening, and all of them are the nous. With Marcus Aurelius she adds that all people are siblings, children of the same nous.

Another angle

Nous is the first emanation of the One: cosmic consciousness and wisdom, the Platonic name for Heraclitus' fire and Logos. It is fluid and unified rather than a thing, and it 'cools' into soul to play the game of matter, so the body is the vehicle of the soul and the soul the vehicle of nous. True self-knowledge means recognising this fiery nous that wears the soul; her best modern Greek word for it is συνειδητότητα, awareness. Yet she also stresses that what finally awakens is beyond mind, and in her Nativity reading Joseph is the doubting mind.

Another angle

Nous is not the calculating mind (λογιστικόν), which is only a sub-function; it is awareness itself, whoever perceives your thoughts, the charioteer. It is the true perceiver behind every sense ('mind sees and mind hears', to which she adds 'mind smells, mind tastes'), the soul's core, symbolised by the Circle of the Same. In her reading of myth, infant Zeus nursed by Amalthea is our nous being fed so that it remembers itself.

Roots

ναῦς (ship)

Mind as a ship, or a wave, on the ocean of the infinite. Athena’s reading

  • Parmenides

Cosmos and the One

λόγος

Logos

lógos

In Athena’s teaching

Logos has many meanings she draws out with her audience (cause, ratio, speech, analogy, promise, reckoning), and every vibration of spacetime is a logos, a ratio shaping the energy of the whole. With Heraclitus she insists the Logos is one and common (ξυνός, with upsilon, not ξινός, 'sour'), though most people think they have a private understanding. The fire of Heraclitus is Logos, primordial consciousness, mostly unspoken (ἄρρητος). Politically, following Aristotle, the political is the distinctive property of logos: our capacity to judge just and unjust.

Another angle

Logos in her teaching is not thinking. In the Pythagoras lesson it is first a ratio, a:b, the number behind every frequency, and then the energy of consciousness itself, the ancient νοῦς that perceives thoughts and emotions, observes and creates. It is one and common to all, the κοινὸς λόγος of Heraclitus, which the Greeks of 1940 joined when they left their borders behind.

Another angle

In Heraclitus's sense the logos is the consciousness through which we perceive even our own personhood, and on waking we find it one and common. She insists that logos is not mind: it shows itself through the mind without being exhausted by it. As discursive reasoning, though, logos is multiple and plunges into number, so it must give way before the simple One.

Athena connects it to

  • Ever-living fire

    The ever-living fire is Logos.

  • Nous

    For the Platonists the same is Nous.

  • Heraclitus

    His Logos is common to all.

  • The political

    The political is logos in action.

  • Cosmos

    The cosmos is ἔλλογος, endowed with logos.

  • Consciousness

    Logos is directly linked to consciousness.

  • The One

    Discursive logos cannot reach the One

  • Hellenic meditation

    Dialogismos is consciousness moving through logos

The good life

ἀλήθεια

Truth

alḗtheia

In Athena’s teaching

Truth for her is simple and has no content: it is a state, not a set of propositions or rules ('not the Ten Commandments'), and propositions are true only by participation (μέθεξις) in it. She reads ἀλήθεια as non-forgetting or non-sleep, hears in 'αλ' a root of light as in ἥλιος, and tentatively sees an anagram of θήλεια, female, because truth keeps giving birth. Truth does not come to you; you come to the truth, which waits here already.

Another angle

Truth is a state of consciousness, not an opinion, an angle or a list of propositions. Its first etymology is the removal of λήθη, forgetting, so truth is subtractive, like death: you strip away rather than add. It is often paradoxical, παρὰ τὴν δόξαν, because the cave is the realm of opinion and no opinion as such can be true. In the Sun simile truth is the immaterial light of the Good, which she distinguishes from mere reality.

Another angle

Plato calls the light of the Good ἀλήθεια: it mediates between the One and our intellection, as sunlight mediates between sun and eye. The ancients spoke of 'touching truth' (ἐφάπτεσθαι τῆς ἀληθείας), and she hears in the verb both touching and being set alight.

Roots

ἀ- (not) + λήθη (forgetting)

Truth is subtractive: un-forgetting what we always were. standard

    Philosophy touches and rekindles truth.

    Only what does not decay is true.

  • Wisdom

The path

λήθη

Lethe, forgetting

lḗthē

In Athena’s teaching

Lethe, forgetting, is what the soul drinks on its descent: it falls from the ever-being into the illusion of the body-tomb-cave. The chains of the cave are λήθη, and the prisoners sleep in the cosmic dream. Asked what is opposite to Being, she says nothing is: within Being there is only the possibility of forgetting itself, and Lethe is the price God pays to manifest and play. Truth, which says 'change', is almost unbearable to someone still in λήθη.

Another angle

Λήθη is the poison of ignorance we drink when we incarnate without παιδεία: we forget we are the One, identify with the part and the body, and from that come desire, attachment and suffering. It is a veil to lift through γνῶθι σαυτόν. In the 28 October talk she reads ἠλίθιος, the idiot, as someone who lives 'in lethe', having forgotten that he is one with his fellow citizens and with everything.

    Forgetting is the only 'opposite' of Being.

    God as a child forgets himself to play and return.

  • Death and the practice of dying

    Forgetting is the soul's death into the body.

  • Aletheia, unforgetting

    Truth is the lifting of lethe

  • The idiotes

    The idiot is the one who lives in lethe

  • Recollection (anamnesis)

    Recollection undoes forgetting

The path

δεύτερη γέννηση

Second birth of the soul

défteri génnisi

In Athena’s teaching

The Orphic, Pythagorean, Eleusinian and Platonic traditions call the awakening of consciousness, while still in the body, a second birth, and she reads Christmas and the ancient Heliougenna as its festival. She maps it as a real pregnancy: a hidden conception below the radar of senses and mind, gestation nourished by love, teaching and virtue, labour pains with a midwife-teacher, a sudden birth into light, then nourishment and strengthening. The newborn is a revelation of what we always were, new and always ancient. Even knowledge follows this pattern: it must be conceived, carried and born in you.

Another angle

The cave is womb and tomb, so leaving it is both a death and a second birth, a resurrection (ἀνάστασις). The soul that hears the call of return is gestated in the middle stage and reborn into the divine level, arriving 'suddenly'. Yet the second birth is not really a birth: you recognise that what you are was never born, never dies, and was never other than the infinite self of the All.

Another angle

At the winter solstice nature strips itself, which is why Heracles, the Sun and, in the later appropriation, Christ are born then. In the soul this is the birth of the inner hero or sun after the descent: the three days the sun 'stands' mean the hero is sown, gestated and born, and 25 December is the birth of the sun. The new birth is your own truth shining, the birth of the χρηστός (useful) human who has found their true need and can benefit all beings.

The path

ἐξαίφνης

The sudden

exaíphnēs

In Athena’s teaching

Ἐξαίφνης, Plato's 'suddenly', is her favourite Platonic word in the podcast: the moment the prisoner is released, or the soul is born into light when its hour is ripe. It does not depend on the human mind but on cosmic law (νομοτέλεια); other traditions call it providence, and it belongs to mystery, which holds the highest place in philosophy. It can come as loss, divorce, ruin or depression, or as an inspiration and the love of one's life, a 'good suddenly'. Either way it shakes a boxed, repetitive life awake.

Another angle

Plato, she says, uses the 'much-longed-for' ἐξαίφνης three times in the cave: the breaking of the chains and every stage of awakening happen suddenly, and Plato does not explain how. Yet the sudden is preceded by long preparation, so awakening is both gradual and sudden. She identifies the ἐξαίφνης with the soul's ripe hour, also called grace.

Another angle

Awakening arrives 'suddenly', the Platonic and Socratic ἐξαίφνης: it cannot be controlled or triggered like pressing a code, because its cause does not lie in the one trying. It is ἀμήχανον, not the product of time, method or knowledge, and is sometimes called divine grace or the Χάριτες. Yet, citing a teacher she calls 'the Indian Socrates', she adds that the suddenness is preceded by long preparation and ripening.

The path

ὑπέρβασις

Transcendence

hypérbasis

In Athena’s teaching

Transcendence is the first of the two movements of philosophy: closing the eyes (μύω), turning away from becoming and finding the One 'beyond'. She calls the belief that truth lies somewhere else a useful 'intermediate falsehood' that helps the soul turn inward. It corresponds to leaving the cave, deconstructing every conjecture, belief and even idea, up to the mystics' 'devouring fire'. But the soul cannot stay above, so transcendence is only half of initiation.

Another angle

In the Neoplatonic formula she cites, enlightenment is transcendent, 'I leave the material', but this is only half: remaining only in the absolute is still dualism. The Good itself is 'beyond' (ἐπέκεινα) knowledge and being.

The path

ἐμμένεια

Immanence

emméneia

In Athena’s teaching

Immanence is the second and longer movement: returning to the cave to recognise that the One remains in everything, here and now. She glosses ἐμμένεια as ἐν + μένω, the One that dwells everywhere, and illustrates it with Odysseus who, after reaching Ithaca, must still slay the suitors, that is, bring light to old habits and programming and integrate them. In daily life it means seeing the One at the tax office, on Taxisnet, in emails and morning coffee. The freed return out of love and justice and live on the razor's edge of the One and the many.

Another angle

Leaving the cave is not the end: the circle closes only when the freed one descends into becoming, not only from compassion but because the apprenticeship is incomplete until then. The Neoplatonists called enlightenment transcendent and also ἐμμένεια, 'remaining in'. Back in the cave one sees that cave and Good are not two, that all is the Good, and that even illusion is awakening that forgets itself.

Another angle

The Neoplatonists debated whether the One is in the world or beyond it, and Plato can be read both ways: the cave points to transcendent Ideas, while Diotima and the Phaedrus show beauty passing through everything. She holds that immanence characterises Hellenism more: God is everywhere and in everyone. This is why the Greeks engaged with polis and art, and why she links lingering transcendentalism to the abuse of nature.

The path

θάνατος

Death and the practice of dying

thánatos

In Athena’s teaching

From the One's perspective, birth into the body is a death and physical death is a return. The first definition of philosophy (Phaedo 64) is μελέτη θανάτου, practice of dying, but the death she means is the death of illusion and of the personality, dis-identifying from the body rather than leaving it. It is a daily process, removing one identification at a time, which is why Socrates says both 'dying' and 'being dead'. For those below the freed one has died, for those above he was born, and when he returns he seems risen from the dead.

Another angle

For her there is no death, only sleep, dream and awakening. Life is the divine dream of Hestia, essence, and death ends the dream: a transition, a λύσις or untying of the cords between soul and body, which calls for courage and clarity and should be prepared for in peacetime. In the Platonic talks death is also what the philosopher rehearses while alive: the death of the illusory self, after which one 'simply goes on being'.

Soul and mind

ψυχή

Soul

psychḗ

In Athena’s teaching

The soul is the vehicle of nous, formed when fiery nous 'cools'; she plays on ψυχή and ψύχω, to cool. It contains the body rather than the reverse: the Timaeus has the soul embracing the body, and what lies outside the body is our aura. In her reading the soul is ἀγαθοειδής, Good-like, carrying a little fiery sun, and in Plato the soul, not the body, is the true subject of politics. It descends by putting on tunics and ascends by taking them off until it is naked.

Another angle

Following the Timaeus and Proclus, she teaches that the soul is not an object like an invisible bottle but self-moving motion, 'a verb, not a noun': two harmonised circular orbits, the Same and the Other, crossing in a χ. The body is inside the soul, not the soul inside the body, and the part of the soul beyond the body is what we now call the aura. Its essence (οὐσία) is never disturbed by what happens to it; only its revolutions are.

Another angle

Soul is localised consciousness, energy cooled relative to the divine fire (she links ψυχή to ψύχω, to cool), and it in turn projects matter. Following Pythagoras she says we are divine souls having a dreamlike human experience. The soul has faculties to study (mind, heart, will and appetite; Plato's three parts), and the Odyssey is the archetypal map of its descent and return.

ψύχω (to cool)

Soul is fiery nous that has cooled; separate selves are ice cubes. Athena’s reading

Cosmos and the One

τὸ ἕν

The One

tò hén

In Athena’s teaching

The One is the ultimate nature of self and cosmos in the Orphic-Platonic-Pythagorean line she calls ancestral: ineffable (ἄρρητον), unknowable (ἄγνωστον), ungraspable (ἄληπτον) and unparticipated (ἀμέθεκτον). It is not a 'something' but an over-full nothing, a boundless radiance that is transcendent and immanent at once: all is in it and it is in all. It shines through every form like one light through the windows of many rooms, and it waits for us to see it rather than us waiting for it.

Another angle

The One is the ineffable source, before even awareness, from which everything cascades and which is present in everything. Philosophy's goal has four names for one end (eudaimonia, gnosis, union and knowledge of the true self), and union is the close of a divine love affair in which two collapse into one. It is less a gain than a remembering, as in the Meno's recollection (ἀνάμνησις), and it requires shedding everything we are not.

Another angle

The One is not a lifeless abstraction but living, rational, self-aware divine consciousness, the source from which all forms rise and to which they return. It is not far away: following Plotinus, it waits for us, and we only remove what covers it. All the talks rest on the Heraclitean principle that the One is in all and all is one, so a self that is separate, a 'private' interest or a bordered nation is a form of sleep.

The path

γνῶθι σαυτόν

Know thyself

gnôthi sautón

In Athena’s teaching

She reads Apollo's Delphic command in two stages. First we take it to mean knowing our personality, preferences, body and the three parts of the soul, and that stage is valid. But at the level of being it asks us to know THE self, which is one in the universe: 'know that which knows', the observer who has thoughts, emotions and a body but is none of them. It is the foundational precept that turns the soul's eye inward, and a life not lit by it is, she says, harder than the effort of self-knowledge.

Another angle

Apollo's own precept at Delphi, which she reads as the god's riddle in place of a welcome: if you want to know me, know yourself. Joined with the cryptic E ("you are"), it says you already are what you seek. It is her standard advice to anyone: turn attention from outside to inside and keep asking who you are, because the self is the one foundation that cannot be taken away.

Another angle

She reads the Delphic maxim not as 'study your separate personality' but as Apollo calling consciousness to turn its eye on itself and know itself as pure knowing, the one Self. The command is singular ('thyself', not 'yourselves'), and she says the elided inscription could also read 'know it'. It marries ontology (σαυτόν: who am I) and epistemology (γνῶθι: how do I know), and whoever follows it finds that the one they thought they were does not exist.

Roots

γνῶθι (know) + σ' αὐτόν (?) (thyself, or 'it')

Cosmos and the One

ἥλιος

The Sun

hḗlios

In Athena’s teaching

In her reading of Plato's Sun simile, which she calls 'Platonic trigonometry', the eye is the most sun-like organ and stores the sun's light; likewise the soul is Good-like and carries a small fiery sun within. The sun is self-luminous while objects are lit by another, and it causes growth without being any of them, as the Good causes knowledge. Its light is truth and its heat is eros. The goal is a stability beyond the solstices, the 'ever-living sun', from whose point of view there is no waxing or waning.

Another angle

The sun is the visible symbol of the pure One and of spirit, so dismissing ancient 'sun worship' as primitive is, for her, an ignorant reading. In the Cave the sun is the Good, and the Sun above the Ideas is her image of the One beyond even the Ideas. After awakening there is no 'awakened person', only the Sun; and your inner sun was never in danger, since it never took part in the drama and only shines.

Another angle

She walks through the Sun simile as the key to the Cave: eye, visible objects and sun form a triangle, and light is the 'third kind' that makes sight possible. The sun does not put sight into the eye but activates a power already there, which for her defines education. Its lord is Apollo, who takes us away from the many.

Cosmos and the One

φῶς

Light

phôs

In Athena’s teaching

Light is her constant image of spirit: the One is a boundless radiance (φωταύγεια, διαύγεια) that spreads like light through the windows of many rooms while staying one. The soul feeds on light, λόγος and realisations, and words are small vehicles carrying that light. She distinguishes three lights by their roots: sensible (ἡλ-, as in ἥλιος), spiritual (ἑλ-, as in Ἕλλην) and uncreated (the third root is uncertain).

Another angle

Light is the mediating condition: in the visible field it lets the eye see, and in the intelligible field its name is truth. To think something is like lighting it so that it becomes intelligible. In the end she says there are not two, light and darkness: darkness is light very much dimmed.

Another angle

Every light is an outflow (ἀπορροή) of fire and presupposes a fire, so in Corinth she moves 'from the gates of light to the source of light'. In the Sun simile light is the hidden fourth term, the 'third kind': without it we see nothing, yet we never see light itself, only objects. She derives φαίνεσθαι, to appear, from φῶς: whatever appears is light woven into forms through the Ideas, like the single light on a cinema screen.

Cosmos and the One

τὸ ὄν / τὸ μὴ ὄν

Being and non-being

tò ón / tò mḕ ón

In Athena’s teaching

Following Parmenides, only what always is, is; for the ancients 'is not' means 'is not true', not 'does not exist'. Whatever rises and sets, sometimes is and sometimes is not, has the quality of non-being: bodies, thoughts, emotions, war and peace, economic booms and busts. Hence Parmenides' reversal: what seems to be is not, and what seems not to be (the invisible, intelligible) truly is. Being has no opposite; being and non-being are not two but one.

Another angle

What she finds most innovative in the similes is that the five modes of knowing correspond to Plato's ontology, five functions or levels of being, so the Cave is a synthesis of epistemology and ontology. On the ontological side the shadows 'seem to exist but do not', being only an emanation or echo of formed objects.

Another angle

She derives Ismenios from ἴσμεν, 'we know', which echoes ἐσμέν, 'we are': at the fourth step we know being. The archer's focus, ἑστία, is οὐσία. Seekers must not confuse the phenomenon with the essence.

Cosmos and the One

γίγνεσθαι

Becoming

gígnesthai

In Athena’s teaching

Becoming is the realm where nothing stays, so everything dies every moment: we live but do not live. She draws it under a 'T' on the board, below the world of rest, as Plato's world of otherness where the pairs of opposites live, and links it to water and Poseidon, the sea of emotions and beliefs. It is a mirror showing an inverted image, a 'drama of the mind' that sees dualistically. Pain within becoming is the alarm clock telling the soul to change.

Another angle

Becoming is Heraclitus' river into which the soul's circles are plunged at birth, a 'first baptism' she also sees in Odysseus crossing Poseidon's waves. Nothing in this world of relativity can describe awakening, and paideia turns the soul from it toward Being. Yet becoming is not evil: it is the moving god called matter, the stage where divine qualities pass from potential to actual. The Titans, from τείνω, are its tensions pulling us off centre.

Another angle

Plato adds a third category between Being and non-being: becoming, what 'is and is not', permanent now but soon a memory in the archives of the universal mind. Only what does not change meets the criterion of truth, so body, emotions, desires and thoughts all fail it. Becoming is also the middle stage of the path, the apprenticeship and pregnancy where the soul turns, and eudaimonia cannot be invested in it.

Ways of knowing

φιλοσοφία

Philosophy

philosophía

In Athena’s teaching

For her, philosophy is a lived spiritual path whose aim is the fulfilment of human nature: to be whole, free and happy. It starts as a love affair, an Eros for truth, and the mind serves only its first steps before it must let go into what contains it; wisdom is not acquired but activated, the clarity of our own being knowing itself. What universities teach today (arguments, polemics, the history of ideas) is in her view only the shell of what its founders defined as a path of awakening.

Another angle

Philosophy for her is not a scholastic training in logic and argument, which is what it 'degenerated into', but a path to touch truth and a practice of death. Pythagoras coined the word as φιλότης toward wisdom, so it starts in the heart with the art of loving. Its aim is union with the Monad, and it moves in two beats: death and rebirth, or awakening and then embodying it as work in the world.

Another angle

Philosophy in its ancient sense is eros for wisdom (φιλότης + σοφία), aiming at union with wisdom rather than mental knowledge, and Aristotle called it the science of sciences. It is a gift we give ourselves because every concept carries light to the soul, but it must become a path of steps toward eudaimonia and not a mental 'sport'. Philosophy is born where being and becoming cross: wholly lost in becoming we are mechanical, and in pure eternity there is nothing to say.

Roots

φιλότης (love and eros) + σοφία (wisdom)

Philosophy is an erotic longing to unite with wisdom, not to know about it. standard

politikḗ

In Athena’s teaching

For the Greeks politics is human nature, not a contract: we are by nature political animals, and the polis exists by nature, prior even to family and individual. So 'I'm not political' is itself a political stance, a frustration of that nature, and today's depoliticisation goes with a 'de-naturalisation'. Plato's polis mirrors the citizen's soul (her 'psycho-politics'), the lawgiver shapes character, and the true polity's shared purpose is awakening. Real participation means judging and ruling together in spaces of logos, not a four-yearly 'political ritual'.

Another angle

Politics here is a stage of consciousness: after union, one returns to the many to harmonise them for the common good. Socrates was the true political man walking the agora, condemned by pseudo-politicians who loved money and power, and she asks from what vision anyone can govern who does not know who they are. The last step, Leschenorios, is a life shared in dialogue for the common good: 'not I but we'. The eros talk adds that even political relationships are erotic in nature.

Another angle

Politics for her starts in the soul and returns to the world. The highest Pythagorean initiation was political, and eudaimonia is collective, the goal of the polity. She derives πολιτική from πόλος, pole, so every city is a field of forces that draws energies according to the inner state of its people. True politics is a «No» to vice and ego, attunement to the common logos, then a return to build foundations in which a civilisation blossoms.

Thinkers

Ἀριστοτέλης

Aristotle

Aristotélēs

In Athena’s teaching

Aristotle appears as Alexander's teacher, who gave him εὖ ζῆν, and as the source of her political anthropology: man is by nature a political animal, the polis exists by nature, and the citizen shares in judging and ruling. She uses his principle that science starts from 'what it is' (τί ἐστι), his view that εὖ ζῆν is the purpose of life and of politics, and his claim that the Good moves things 'as the beloved'. She says that for him γενναιότητα is the first moral virtue.

Another angle

Aristotle supplies her with ἐντελέχεια and the olive seed, eudaimonia as the human entelechy, virtue that brings eudaimonia when sustained, the innate appetite (ὄρεξις) to learn, and 'the human being is a political animal' against the social contract. His On the Soul she calls the starting point of modern psychology. In the radio interview she adds that Newton's 'giants' were chiefly Aristotle, a claim she bases on his notebooks.

Another angle

She uses Aristotle for the logic of ends: eudaimonia is the final cause behind every act, with nothing behind it, and it is our ἐντελέχεια. His seed of walnut or oak, carrying the whole tree and an impulse to grow even in poor soil, is her image of the soul tending to eudaimonia because it comes from it. He also supplies 'the human is a political animal' and calls philosophy the science of sciences; she notes he studied at Plato's school from 17 to 37.

The path

ἀφύπνιση

Awakening

afýpnisi

In Athena’s teaching

For her the fashionable word 'awakening' belongs to consciousness, not to the body (though it finally includes it) and not even to the soul, whose awakening is only one stage. Reality is already awake as living logos and self-knowing nous; only we sleep and wake, so nothing changes in the world and everything changes in us. It is not a spectacle of visions or miracles but an often unnoticed inner shift of vision, like veils lifting, and she maps it as five ordered steps named after Apollo. In the eros talk the erotic path is itself a path of awakening, which she equates with eudaimonia and freedom.

Another angle

For her, awakening is not an experience, vision, energy event, emotion or insight, because every experience happens inside a limit while awakening concerns the infinite. It is the beholding (θέασις) of the One: a recognition without knowledge, a witness in which the separate 'you' disappears and you see you were always awake. It cannot be manufactured by time or method; it comes suddenly, usually after long ripening. The modern word stands for what the ancients called λύσις, liberation and εὐδαιμονία.

Another angle

She defines awakening as an ineffable realisation, a beholding in which nothing changes: only the true nature of the self and of the whole as one is seen. Because the word implies a sleeper, she prefers the ancient θέασις, and she calls 'the awakened person' one of the greatest illusions, since such an identity keeps a gap between the ego and the pure 'I am'. It is not a political revelation, an energy experience or an out-of-body state.

Cosmos and the One

ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ τὸ ποιούμενον

Non-duality

ho poiētḕs kaì tò poioúmenon

In Athena’s teaching

She reads the Greek tradition as non-dual: in Plotinus' witness the seer and the seen are one, a union (ἕνωσις) other cultures call yoga. Diotima's negative description of absolute beauty is for her 'a wonderful non-dual description', the most language can do beyond the duality it is built for. She also rejects the dualist Plato in which sensible and intelligible are enemies; for her they are one continuum, and at the deepest level the inside and outside of the cave are one.

Another angle

She teaches two ways to live, polarised and a-polarised, and coins the verb 'απολώσου': get un-polarised. Apollo takes no pole and no side, and removing the poles lets the One appear. Dual statements are both true and untrue (her 'right or left?' gesture), and the three approaches to a god are all true at once. In the eros talk: 'there is the individual and there is no individual', and in reality there are no others.

Another angle

She argues that a large non-dual corpus lies hidden in the Presocratic, Socratic and Neoplatonic texts, above all Plotinus, ignored first by Christian theology and then by reductionist academia. Greek thought contains both a direct path and a graded education. Duality and non-duality are not opposed but dance together, and her ontology is a non-dual account of the dual world.

Cosmos and the One

ἡλιοστάσιο

Winter solstice

iliostásio

In Athena’s teaching

The winter solstice, when the sun seems to stand still and then climbs again, is for her the soul's deepest dive into the body, the longest night and 'dark night of the soul' before rebirth. Christmas falls four days later because for the Pythagoreans four is establishment, the cube: what was performed in the depths is consolidated. She treats solstices and equinoxes as days of highest energetic inflow around which the ancient festival calendar was built. Yet from the sun's own point of view there is no waxing or waning at all.

Another angle

She reads the four astronomical turnings as energy gates whose visible pattern mirrors movements of consciousness, on the Hermetic principle 'as below, so above'. Each turning (τροπή) releases food (τροφή) for the soul. At an equinox the soul's two circles meet, a moment of balance and sowing; at a solstice they are farthest apart, a crisis that can birth the inner hero. They are fertile conditions, not requirements: the best moment is always now.

Soul and mind

σῶμα

Body

sôma

In Athena’s teaching

Life in the body is, from the One's view, the field of death: σῶμα σῆμα, the body as tomb, the Cave, the soul's winter solstice. Yet awakening happens without leaving the body, by dis-identifying from it. The body is the vehicle of the soul and is contained by it, not the reverse. Politically she criticises the modern individual understood as a body, the subject of science and biopolitics, set in the place of soul and consciousness.

Another angle

She inverts the usual picture: the soul does not enter the body; the body enters the soul and is embraced by it. Plato calls the body a seat of continual inflow and outflow, porous, breathing, always exchanging with the great river of life. The body does not sense; it is a set of gates through which the river's motions reach the soul, which is why a body without soul senses nothing. The soul's overflow beyond the body is the aura.

Another angle

Opinions, factions and ideologies rest on the belief that 'I am the body and others are bodies'. Racial origin refers only to the body, so dividing people by race identifies the human with the body, a materialist way of seeing.

Ways of knowing

σοφία

Wisdom

sophía

In Athena’s teaching

Wisdom is living awareness (ἐπίγνωσις) in contact with the here and now, where life itself tells you what is what. Using the Cratylus she ties σοφία to light and to ὁρμή, motion, being connected with an ever-changing energy, and σύνεσις to 'going along with' things like an alert general. The dry soul is the wisest, warmed by the fire of the Good. Pythagoras, she says, knew that love (φιλότης) and wisdom go together.

Another angle

Wisdom is linked with light, the light of understanding and realisation (her etymology, flagged uncertain). Philosophy seeks to merge with it, not to collect information about it. Her chosen line from Plato sets its moral condition: all knowledge severed from justice and the other virtues is cunning, not wisdom.

Another angle

She draws her first practical proposal from the 'sophia' in philosophy: observe the mind, do not take what we believe for granted, and open a space between what I think and the I that watches it. 'There lies the key.'

Roots

φῶς (light) + ὁρμή (rush, motion (Laconian))

Wisdom is being connected with an ever-moving energy (Cratylus). Athena’s reading

The good life

ἐλευθερία

Freedom

eleuthería

In Athena’s teaching

She asks us to celebrate freedom not as a memory but as the present state of our existence. Splitting ἐλευθερία, with an omega slipped under its omicron, she finds light (Ἑλ), the good (εὖ) and the eros that warms (θέρ-, ἔρως): freedom is eros, which is why a «Yes» must follow the «No». In the other talks freedom is what the free hands of the cave prisoners already hold and what self-inquiry finds at the root of awareness.

Another angle

Freedom is inner before it is outer: Marcus Aurelius and Diogenes show one can be free even in prison, and every situation has an 'exit of freedom'. In her reading ἐλευθερία 'has ἔρως inside it': people make their greatest revolutions out of love, as the fighters of 1821 were drunk on love of freedom. Recognising one's true nature as fire and as the Good is freedom and leaving the cave. The reborn soul is free and joyful like a child, but a wise child.

Another angle

Freedom is one of the universal aims philosophy fulfils, with wholeness and happiness. The Golden Verses say that if you leave the body for the free aether you become an immortal god: if, not when, so liberation is available now whenever we stop clinging to the body. Later Hellenic teachings, she says, describe an inner freedom and a happiness free from circumstances.

Soul and mind

προαίρεσις

Free will

In Athena’s teaching

In her reading the prisoners of the cave are chained by legs and neck but not by the hands, and hands stand for free will, an extension of the heart, which can never be subjugated. So the first ingredient of liberation is wanting it: no mother, partner or child can change you from outside, except perhaps divine grace. 'Even the universe respects free will', so leave the door open a little. Wanting starts to turn the wheels of soul and life and draws events.

Another angle

Plato deliberately leaves the prisoners' hands free, and she reads the hands as free will, as in 'it's in your hands'. Even while bound, something in us has never been bound and never will be: the capacity to decide. When the turn comes it is this unmoved, unsubdued part that stands up first, in an ineffable way, saying 'it can't be only this'.

αἰσχύνη / αἰδώς

Respecting shame

In Athena’s teaching

She offers the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβου, 'respect shame', as a healthy alternative to self-flagellation, which she calls a pathological relation to conscience. Αἰδώς is the restraint felt before a wrong act, αἰσχύνη what one feels after it; respecting shame means respecting the self-regulation of justice within you. The ego hides from its Erinyes and from solitude; instead one sees the error, learns, adjusts and moves on. Feeling shame is healthy; feeling nothing is the danger.

Thinkers

Σωκράτης

Socrates

Sōkrátēs

In Athena’s teaching

Socrates' 'I know one thing, that I know nothing' is the method that opens the pores of ἀπορία so Apollo can reveal himself. His daimonion told him only 'make music and work at it', meaning reach the last step of harmonising the many, and he walked the agora as a true political man until pseudo-politicians condemned him. In the eros talk he learns from Diotima, calls the path an erotic pedagogy, and teaches that health is inner peace and illness an inner civil war.

Another angle

Not an anti-mystical rationalist but a mystic of the agora: an Eleusinian initiate who called Diotima his greatest teacher and meditated all night at Potidaea. His novelty was an anthropocentric turn, bringing spiritual realisation down into ethics, law and politics. His knowing that he knows nothing is the same letting go of mind that Plotinus describes, and he defined the philosopher as a lover of truth, warning that knowledge without justice is dangerous.

Another angle

Socrates is the figure behind most of her readings: he defines παιδεία as the turning of the soul, calls death λύσις and philosophy a practice of death, speaks of the eyes of the soul, and works as a midwife, not a teacher. In her retelling he meets death like an Olympic athlete stepping out to perform what he trained for, and his daimonion's 'make music' becomes the Pythagorean programme. For him, she says, the way to truth is subtraction, not acquisition.

She calls him 'grandfather Parmenides', near whom Socrates sprouted. From him she takes that only what always is, is, and non-being never was, and the reversal: what seems to be is not, what seems not to be, is. Thinkers

Πλωτῖνος

Plotinus

Plōtînos

In Athena’s teaching

'Beloved Plotinus' supplies her key descriptions of awakening: the seer is one with the seen, so it is not even a vision; you do not become someone else, 'another' wrapped around you departs; and the One waits for us to see it. His light passing from room to room images the one essence in many forms, and his 'let us flee to the beloved fatherland' turns the Odyssey into the soul's homecoming. She pairs him with θέασις and θέωσις, and with the call to become σύμπας.

Another angle

She carries the Enneads with her and reads 'there were not two... not a vision but a union' as the best description of beholding. Plotinus calls the One your true self, says whoever unites with the One was always the One, and points to silence. She thinks he is little studied because his clearly non-dual teaching cannot be understood without being lived.

Another angle

Plotinus supplies her highest statements about the One and the Good: it is nowhere, yet there is nowhere it is not; it comes 'like one who never left'; and when you know the Good you recognise it as yourself (Ennead VI.9). She also takes from him that nous is fluid and unified, not a thing. She reads Kazantzakis' 'even the One does not exist' as reaching the highest vision Plotinus describes.

Thinkers

Πρόκλος

Proclus

Próklos

In Athena’s teaching

She speaks of 'beloved and fully awakened Proclus'. From him she takes that the soul descends by synthesis, adding foreign tunics, and ascends by analysis, removing what does not belong to it until it is naked (quoting a Chaldean oracle). His procession and return (πρόοδος, ἐπιστροφή) frame her two movements of transcendence and immanence. She also cites his derivation of the Titans from τείνω and, uncertainly, of Dionysus as 'two minds'.

Another angle

Proclus is her guide to the Timaeus: newborn souls cannot yet navigate embodiment, sense turbulence disturbs the soul's revolutions but never its essence, and the soul is two circles in a χ. He supplies the ideal of the 'naked soul' stripped of false identifications, and the reading of heroes' parentage as soul-astronomy ('Proclus scored, Greeks 1-0'). He stands in her lineage after Plotinus and Iamblichus.

Another angle

Proclus gives her two key ideas in the Ares lesson: incarnation as a 'divine sleep' and 'divine dream', and, in his commentary on the Republic, the contrast between Athena's war by union and Ares' war by division. In the second-birth talk she groups him with Plato, Socrates and Plotinus as agreeing that νοῦς halts at the threshold of the true, beyond which one must leap.

Thinkers

Διοτίμα

Diotima

Diotíma

In Athena’s teaching

Socrates' teacher, a priestess from Arcadia in her account, and in the Symposium the only surviving text where we see a woman teaching. Diotima defines philosophy as a path of Eros and lays out a ladder of love that Potari counts as seven levels, rising from interpersonal to political and cosmic love. Her erotic pedagogy is for Potari the education every age needs, and she also cleansed the karmic residue of the plague in Athens.

Another angle

Diotima was Socrates' woman teacher, and she taught him that the path of self-knowledge, philosophy, awakening and freedom is an erotic journey. From her comes the claim that the goal of eros coincides with the goal of human life. Athena stresses that the wisest man had a woman as his teacher.

Another angle

Diotima of Mantinea, a priestess, was Socrates' teacher, which she says schools do not tell us. Her ladder of eros rises from bodily attraction to souls, political love, the sciences, the arts and finally divine eros, merging into the ocean of life, an erotic union with the One. She also teaches that humans are pregnant in soul even more than in body, gestating logos and virtue. Potari attributes to her a 'sea of truth', which she reads as a fiery sea where all is united.

Gods and myths

Ἀπόλλων

Apollo

Apóllōn

In Athena’s teaching

Apollo, god of light and clarity, is for her the god of awakening itself. She builds a whole talk on nine keys: the four etymologies of his name in Plato's Cratylus and the five cult names in Plutarch's On the E at Delphi, read as five ordered steps with the etymologies as the passages between them. Her favourite reading is ἀ + πολλῶν, 'not of the many': he takes no side and removes the poles, and when the many go the One appears. Every etymology of his name, she says, has a subtractive and an additive side.

Another angle

Following Plutarch and Plotinus, she says the Pythagoreans' code name for the One was Apollo, read as ἀ- + πολλῶν, 'not of the many': the boundless radiance beyond polarities, the 'zero' where opposing forces cancel. The philosophers also called νῦν, 'now', a name of Apollo. At Delphi it is Apollo who asks consciousness to know itself, and he shares Delphi with Dionysus, as the Same shares the soul with the Other.

Another angle

She reads Ἀπόλλων as ἀ- plus πολλῶν, 'not of the many': in his highest aspect he symbolises the One, the single pole of the universe, which is why he is always shown young (unity is youth). Lord of sun and fire, he calls us at Delphi to know ourselves, that is, to find the inner fire. Leto, fleeing Lethe, bears him on Delos, 'the manifest', after Artemis. At Delphi he shakes hands with Dionysus, an image of the god-man.

Roots

ἀ- (not) + πολλῶν (of the many)

Apollo is the One beyond polarity, inviting us out of dualism into unity. Athena’s reading

Gods and myths

Διόνυσος

Dionysus

Diónysos

In Athena’s teaching

Dionysus' birth at the winter solstice (the Dionysia, Heliougenna) is the ancient form of the sacred infant's birth, and Heraclitus says Dionysus and Hades are the same. He holds the initiatory mirror: the visible world is an inverted reflection, and the Titans dismember him as daily pulls fragment our attention. As god of theatre he teaches that each of us plays a role but is not the role. She cites a reading of his name as 'two minds' (δύο νοῦς), the dyadic mind that must pass through the drama.

Another angle

Theatre belongs to Dionysus, and life is the cosmic drama in which the One plays all the roles; awakening means playing on 'the stage of Dionysus' consciously and with cheer. In the Titans myth the tensions of becoming tear Dionysus apart until only the heart remains, which Athena (wisdom) saves for rebirth. He holds Delphi in winter while Apollo is away, and she maps him onto the Circle of the Other.

Another angle

Following Plutarch, she says Apollo and Dionysus are one: two states of the universe. Dionysus is the dyadic mind, the one becoming many; Apollo is the universe's fulfilment, the moment it 'catches fire' to return into unity in a luminous, non-material fire. Nietzsche, she tells an audience member, 'began from good premises', but Plutarch already treats the two as one.

Roots

δύο (two) + νοῦς (mind)

Gods and myths

Ἄρης

Ares

Árēs

In Athena’s teaching

She rescues Ares from the hot-headed war god of popular tales. In his higher form he is the upward impulse of birth (Aries, spring, the shoot breaking the soil) and the power that divides in order to restore justice and good order (εὐταξία). Following Proclus she sets him beside Athena: Athena is war by union at the intelligible level, Ares war by division in the sublunar, emotional world, and wisdom always outranks force. Purified and raised on a base of purity, his red fire becomes vital force, boundaries, health, frank speech and the courage the awakened need in the cave, which is why she calls him the god of peace.

Another angle

She rejects the one-dimensional image of Ares as an impulsive, aggressive war god. In her reading he is the god of Peace and of Εὐνομία, good order under law, an inner and outer cosmic force whose higher function guards the Light, the Divine, Balance and Love. In the Orphic Hymn his βία means life-force, vitality and strength (σθένος), not violence. A complete spiritual path must integrate him: we must be fighters on the path of virtue and self-knowledge, which is why Plato's philosophers must also be guardians.

Roots

Gods and myths

Ἑστία

Hestia

Hestía

In Athena’s teaching

In the Orphic sequence Hestia, read as οὐσία, essence, falls asleep into multiplicity and dreams the incarnation, so life is the divine dream and death its end. She is also the nucleus of Olympus around which Ares forms the outer shell. In the Pythagoras lesson the ἑστία is the sacred fire at the centre of the heart: light it before you speak of sacred things, so that the light becomes words.

Another angle

Hestia never leaves the centre of Olympus while the other gods come and go, so she is her image of the Circle of the Same, the still centre of the soul. When 'you' are no longer the centre of your world, the centre becomes Hestia: pure beholding, the One. Your core is a fiery focal point (ἑστία), and the mean (μεσότης) is the hearth of virtue and eudaimonia.

Another angle

Hestia keeps the ever-burning flame at the centre of Olympus, and she derives the name from ἐσσία/οὐσία, essence: our essence is that primordial flame. We have 'got it wet', like Odysseus soaked by Poseidon's waves, but it is always within. Philosophers speak of kindling the inner Hestia, and recollection happens when Hestia is lit at the centre of the mind.

Cosmos and the One

αἰών

Aion, the playing child

aiṓn

In Athena’s teaching

Heraclitus says Aion is a child playing draughts and the kingship is the child's. She reads αἰών as ἀεὶ ὤν, 'the ever-being': the child holds infinite possible scenarios as dice and at each moment manifests a new world or role. This Child was the goal of the Kabeiric mysteries of Samothrace, and the 'kingdom of the child' anticipates the 'kingdom of God'. The reborn soul becomes such a child again, playing freely but wisely, and God forgets himself as a child in order to play and return.

Gods and myths

Ὀδύσσεια

Odyssey

Odýsseia

In Athena’s teaching

The Odyssey is her map of the soul's journey home (νόστος), which she pairs with νόστιμος, 'tasty': nothing is tastier than eudaimonia. Odysseus leaves Circe, Calypso and even the advanced Phaeacians, because high understanding is a station, not the goal: 'as long as you see something, you haven't reached Ithaca'. Her twist is that Odysseus does not return to Ithaca; he wakes up in Ithaca, because he was always there.

Another angle

Not just literature but an archetypal account of the soul: its descent into becoming, its sufferings and lessons, and its νόστος home. The Presocratics, Plato and the Neoplatonists read it theologically, as a code of the soul's path. She reads the hero's name two ways: from ὀδύσσομαι (suffering) and, esoterically, as the journey from the two to the Good to the One.

Another angle

Each soul is an Odysseus travelling from the One into the many and back to Ithaca, and we need companions for the return. The voyage home runs from book Α to Ν; from Ν to Ω he must slay the suitors, meaning bring light to old habits, passions and programming and integrate them, the long immanent stage. Odysseus tied to the mast is the inner axis that holds while fortune's wheel turns, and Odysseus soaked by Poseidon is our inner flame made wet by the passions.

Gods and myths

Δελφοί

Delphi

Delphoí

In Athena’s teaching

'We are the oracle of Delphi': the old, stagnant chthonic forces occupying the sacred space of our soul are the Python in the oracle. At the first step knowledge is still mediated, as when we go to a Pythia who is 'somewhere else'; mantic knowing means becoming the oracle ourselves. There was a lesche at Delphi, the meeting place of the fifth step, and the Delphic γνῶθι σαυτόν names the erotic path.

Another angle

Delphi is where Apollo, lord of sun and fire, calls us to know ourselves, which for her means recognising the inner fire. She draws two maxims from it: γνῶθι σαυτόν, her billboard motto, and αἰσχύνην σέβου, 'respect shame', which she attributes to one of the Seven Sages. At Delphi Apollo and Dionysus shake hands, which she reads as the god-man: divine and human nature as one equation to solve.

Another angle

Delphi is where Apollo inscribes 'know thyself', which she reads as consciousness turning to itself, and 'κόσμιος γίνου', which she reads as 'become cosmic', not 'be polite'. 'Know thyself' is one of about 147 Delphic maxims. Dionysus holds Delphi for the three winter months and Apollo returns at the spring equinox, an image of the two natures uniting.

The path

μυστήρια

The Mysteries

mystḗria

In Athena’s teaching

The Orphic, Eleusinian, Kabeiric and Platonic traditions encode the second birth. She derives initiation (μύησις) from μύω, closing eyes and lips to turn inward, and says from μύησις comes κύησις, pregnancy: initiation is conception, gestation, birth. The Kabeiric procession led to 'the Child', Persephone's story traces descent and return, and the Eleusinian climax fell, she says, at the autumn equinox. Mystery holds the highest place in philosophy.

Another angle

Embedded in philosophy is mystagogy, the hieratic, but not in today's religious sense. It was cut away when the new religion sought a monopoly on the divine, and after Justinian it went underground into alchemists and orders. She calls for putting mystagogy back 'on the central table of the Pythagoreans', without fear, and says we are the first generation in seventeen centuries free to do so.

Another angle

She derives μύησις and μυστήριον from μύω, to close the eyes or mouth: initiation is closing the eyes to phenomena, and a mystery is secret not because it is forbidden but because it cannot be said. The highest grade, ἐποπτεία, is recognising sensible and intelligible as one. No special robe or place is needed, since the world is already God's Telesterion and the senses are its doors.

Cosmos and the One

ἀπορροή

Emanation

aporroḗ

In Athena’s teaching

In her simplified Neoplatonic model, matter flows from soul, soul from nous, and nous from the fiery One: one continuum, drawn as a sphere because all cosmogony happens inside the One. Heraclitus has no creation, only manifestation, a moment when something lights up. Each level is a vehicle (ὄχημα) of the one above: body of soul, soul of nous, nous of fire. Every light likewise is an outflow of fire.

Another angle

The gods flow from the One like a spring gushing water into eddies and droplets. Odysseus' leaving and returning matches the Neoplatonic procession, remaining and return. Zeus keeps generating ideas and natures, and Apollo leads us back from them to the essence.

Soul and mind

αὔη ψυχή

The dry soul

aúē psychḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Heraclitus B118 says the dry soul is wisest and best. She explains αὔη as ἀ- plus ὕω, 'not rained upon': the soul warmed by the fire of the Good, truth and Apollo evaporates the passions, which the tradition calls wet and sticky, each passion a κόλλημα, a sticking. Fear, rage, jealousy and envy soak the soul deeper into Poseidon's waters. The remedy is contact with the forms, the inward turn and the cultivation of virtue and justice.

Ways of knowing

μαιευτική

Maieutics

maieutikḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Socrates' art is midwifery: he speaks only with those already pregnant in soul and helps what is held in potential pass into actuality. The gestation must already have begun in the student; no teacher can do the inner work for you. In the birth of the soul the midwife-teacher pulls one out 'with force' at the ripe hour. Knowledge too is conceived as a seed, carried and delivered with maieutic help.

Another angle

Socrates was a midwife, not a teacher. She recalls (from the Theaetetus, she thinks) that he spoke only with those he saw were pregnant: souls past the first stage of sleep but not yet in contact with Being. Diotima's teaching supports it: humans are pregnant in body but more in soul, with φρόνησις, ἀρετή and finally the true self.

Thinkers

Νίκος Καζαντζάκης

Nikos Kazantzakis

Níkos Kazantzákis

In Athena’s teaching

She loves Kazantzakis and calls him 'the Heraclitus of the modern era'. His Ascetic, subtitled Salvatores Dei, shows her that the path is warlike: we must save God, the divine spark, from our personality and traumas, and its closing prayer that even the One does not exist marks for her the last step to the Source. In the 28 October talk his sense that 'if the earth is not saved, it is my fault' is what she says Greeks felt in 1940.

Another angle

She returns often to Kazantzakis' Ascesis (The Saviours of God). Its end, 'even this One does not exist', is for her not nihilism but the highest vision Plotinus describes, the last step beyond the One. She also uses his 'I follow my deep heartbeat' as the way βίος becomes ζωή, his 'to love means to be lost', and his 'Cry' as the voice of conscience surfacing in solitude.

Soul and mind

πόνος

Pain as a wake-up call

In Athena’s teaching

Pain, loss and grief in becoming are the soul's alarm clock, signals that something must change. Depression can be 'the cry of the soul' to be freed from the prison it built, a 'spiritual surgery' for someone whose mask has stuck, and its long sleep can be a passage from the sleep of routine to waking; she reframes 'depressed' as 'deep rest'. She speaks of her own loss of a loved one, and adds that help may be needed so the person does not get lost there. One may also need to be 'sufficiently disappointed by becoming' for the flame of eros to catch.

Another angle

Pain, she says, is allowed in the drama of the world because it is the perfect motive toward truth. The torment of constant change, things good one moment and bad the next, wears us out until we say 'enough', and the soul, which never moved, keeps sensing that 'something here doesn't add up'. In the Pythagorean principles suffering comes from identifying with the part, and pain finally makes us say 'I am something far greater'.

Another angle

Psychic pain can be a perfect gate: as in training, it hurts and leads to no pain. Athena hears π in πόνος, the sound of pressing (πιέζω): pain presses and pushes, and when nothing else moves us, divine providence presses out of love, so that pain becomes a gate of liberation.

Roots

π (the sound of pressing, as in πιέζω) + ν (unclear in the captions, perhaps νοῦς)

Pain presses and pushes, activating us; when nothing else moves us, providence presses, and pain becomes a gate of liberation. The captions are garbled here. Athena’s readingReconstructed from unclear captions

Cosmos and the One

κόσμος

Cosmos

kósmos

In Athena’s teaching

'This cosmos, the same for all' in Heraclitus means the totality of creation, every ontological level, and she sees parallel universes already implied. It was made by no god or human: it is self-manifesting fire, beyond space and time. The cosmos is ἔλλογος, rational and conscious, governed by mathematical laws that also govern human becoming, which is why our consciousness is collective. Through justice, the subtlest fire, it is always in balance.

Another angle

The Greek cosmos is teleological: nothing is random, and everything born tends toward its purpose. The sensible cosmos mirrors the noetic one ('as below, so above'), and the soul's two circles mirror the celestial equator and the ecliptic. So the Delphic 'κόσμιος γίνου' does not mean good manners but 'recognise your cosmic nature': become whole, Plotinus' σύμπας, the world in you and you in the world.

Another angle

Κόσμος also means ornament: the world is beautiful, ordered by harmony and law. What makes the all (πᾶν) a σύμπαν is the σύν of love, the cohesive force. The cosmos is governed by moral and spiritual as well as material laws, which a wise lawgiver studies and transcribes into ethics.

Roots

κόσμος (order; ornament (κόσμημα))

The world is a jewel, beautiful and ruled by harmony and law. standard

φύσις

Nature

In Athena’s teaching

Greek ethical and political thought turns on living κατὰ φύσιν, according to nature, in a cosmos that is rational. She diagnoses the last two centuries as a 'de-naturalisation' (ἀποφυσικοποίηση): the belief that we are separate from a non-rational nature, the twin of depoliticisation. For the Greeks all is φύσις, which is why 'metaphysics' is not a Greek category but a library label for Aristotle's work placed after the Physics.

Soul and mind

συνειδητότητα

Consciousness

syneidētótēta

In Athena’s teaching

She reads συνείδησις as σύν + εἰδέναι: being present with the knowing, the seeing and self-knowledge, so that we are συνειδότες, witnesses of truth. Consciousness works like a searchlight: wherever its beam turns, it receives that experience. The essence of the world is already consciousness of itself, Aristotle's νόησις νοήσεως, so awakening is our consciousness turning toward what already is. Its clarity, our 'tuning', decides how the god appears to us.

Another angle

Consciousness is one and common, not shut in a box labelled with your name; whoever wakes up sees this, as Heraclitus says. It flows from the One as νοῦς and continues as soul and matter, so there is no gap between mind and matter. She holds that today's physics and cosmology are showing that matter springs from an ocean of consciousness, and she names love as another word for this shared unity.

Another angle

She holds that consciousness is primary and one and is not produced by the brain; matter is a way consciousness arranges itself to appear. The cave is 'a function of my consciousness': what I take myself to be decides how my consciousness works and what world I live in. Yet she also says that what awakening realises goes beyond even consciousness in the ordinary sense, and beyond the mind.

The good life

ἀρετή

Virtue

aretḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Following an etymology she takes from Plato's Cratylus, she reads ἀρετή as 'ever-flowing' (ἀεὶ ῥεῖν): virtue is the soul's energy flowing freely, without blockages. Observing and knowing the soul restores that flow, which is why self-knowledge is therapeutic; in Pythagorean terms the virtues are the right intervals of the soul's music. Ethics is regulating the soul toward ἀρετή, which, sustained over time, brings eudaimonia, and like Heracles at the crossroads we choose it, or vice, at every moment.

Another angle

Virtue is what the soul gestates together with logos (Diotima) and what nourishes the embryo of awakening. In the Leto story Artemis, whom she reads as ἀρετή, is born first, before Apollo the manifest light: out of forgetting comes virtue, then truth. Virtue is the mean that answers the twin errors of nihilism and hedonism, and justice brings one back to it. On the path of virtue, she says, we must be fighters like Ares.

Another angle

She sets out the ancient ladder of virtues as the method of philosophy: first the ethical or political virtues, then the cathartic, then the paradigmatic, culminating in the hieratic or theological virtues found in nearly all ancient philosophers. The Republic teaches how to unite the soul's parts in a fine mean, and justice is the virtue of virtues.

Virtue is the soul's unobstructed flow, which she attributes to Plato. disputedReconstructed from unclear captions

Thinkers

Χριστούγεννα

Christmas and the Nativity

Christoúgenna

In Athena’s teaching

She reads Christmas as the latest coding of the archetype of the sacred infant, behind which stand the Dionysia and the Heliougenna. She decodes the Nativity line by line: the cave is Plato's Cave, the manger is the solar-plexus seat of the irrational powers, the two animals are spleen and liver, Mary (Despoina) is the soul, Joseph the doubting mind, Herod's soldiers the forces threatening the newborn, and the flight into Egypt keeping it hidden. She ends wishing 'Christougenna, Iliougenna, Alithiougenna': birth of Christ, of the sun, of truth.

Another angle

Early theologians appropriated Platonic and Aristotelian elements but could not let philosophy stand as an alternative path to the divine. Some theology put God outside the world and demonised body and desire, which she links to the abuse of nature; the daimon itself was turned into a demon. She stresses respect for all traditions while naming the loss, and notes academia grew out of church institutions.

Another angle

She traces the distortion of philosophy to the post-Christian era and the Middle Ages: the new religion wanted a monopoly on access to the divine, so a path promising union with divinity through philosophy, logic and science had to be cut. Justinian's decree in the 6th century forbade teaching mathematics, the mysteries and theology, sending the knowledge underground.

  • Immanence

  • Daimon

    It turned daimon into demon
