Ways of knowing

ἐπιστήμη

Science and spirit

epistḗmē

In Athena’s teaching

She respects science absolutely, but when the sciences are studied only materialistically, Platonic epistemology places them among convictions and dogmas; even science can harbour fanaticism, as the medical debates of the previous two years showed. With Kuhn she says communities resist paradigm change from emotional investment, not lack of evidence. The ancient aim is to reunite philosophy's science with its spirituality, 'because the source of science is God who ever geometrises'.

Another angle

She derives ἐπιστήμη from ἐπί + ἵσταμαι, standing above and seeing the whole, so nothing that is not holistic is scientific in the ancient sense. In the Greek tradition science and spirituality were one, and she predicts that science, 'sweating but successfully', will within decades prove spirituality and bring a renaissance. The Galileo Commission call she wrote asks what the humanities would look like if consciousness, not matter, is primary.

Another angle

For the Greeks, studying the cosmos meant knowing the mind, nature and body of God: science is the mind's approach to the divine, mysticism the heart's, philosophy the spirit's. Science cannot reach the One, and knowledge detached from justice becomes dangerous, as in environmental damage. She sees physics moving to a consciousness-first paradigm that many scientists resist, like Galileo's colleagues refusing the telescope.

Roots

ἐπί (upon, above) + ἵσταμαι (to stand)

Science is standing above and seeing the whole; whatever is not holistic is not scientific. standard

Soul and mind

ἑαυτός

The true Self

heautós

In Athena’s teaching

The personality (περσόνα) is the sum of changing parts, a role with its costume and name, and identifying with it is the death philosophy undoes. Life is a theatre: the actor (ἠθοποιός) 'makes an ethos' by how he plays, but is not the role, and the task is to recognise who plays all the roles. Justice as 'doing one's own' refers to the one fiery Self, and acting justly is a two-way road to discovering it. The Titans, our outward tendencies, lock us into a role for every stimulus.

Another angle

Knowing yourself has three levels, laid out like a temple: the outer self (body, mind, personality, the story of the small self), the inner self (the soul and its faculties) and the secret self, oneself as the One. To reach the last you become a naked soul, in Proclus's phrase, taking off every role. Material things, even the body, can be taken away, she says, but the self cannot.

Another angle

The true self is the primary essence, the pure One, prior to every predicate such as 'Greek'. Plotinus recognises it as 'the self I always was' and calls the One your true, mystical, or simply everyday self. The suffering self that seems to seek the light is itself a shadow: who seeks the light, the shadow or the light?

    Dionysus is the god of the theatre of roles.

  • Soul

    The soul is the inner self

  • The One

    The secret self is oneself as the One

  • Daimon

    The daimon is the true inner self

The Titans

In Athena’s teaching

The Titans are not bad guys out there but our inner tendencies: following Proclus she derives the name from τείνω, to stretch or tend. Thinkers

Στωικοί

The Stoics

Stōikoí

In Athena’s teaching

From the Stoics she takes ἀταραξία, inner peace as the core of εὖ ζῆν, and ἐκπύρωσις, the periodic ignition of the universe in which the seminal reasons (σπερματικοὶ λόγοι) lie as seeds of all forms. Marcus Aurelius, 'very close to my heart this period', teaches ἀπάθεια: happiness not invested in externals, which she distinguishes from indifference, and he shows one can be free even in prison. An unnamed later Stoic gives her the idea that nothing happens to me without my free will.

Another angle

She cites Marcus Aurelius, 'the enlightened emperor, the Stoic', who ruled an empire at war yet lived the pure One, which the Stoics call the ἡγεμονικόν. From his notes to himself she takes two lessons: do not be 'Caesarified', do not identify with your role; and all people are siblings, children of the same nous.

Thinkers

Πυθαγόρας

Pythagoras

Pythagóras

In Athena’s teaching

Pythagoras is for her the great initiate who coined the word philosophy and defined its aim as union with the Monad, a 'Greek yoga' that joins the Dionysian, Orphic way of the heart with the Apollonian, Ionian way of mind and science. Arriving between a fading priesthood and a rising science, he reformed Greek tradition, and his highest initiation was political. Above all he is a potential of our own soul: she decodes his name until she can say 'you are Pythagoras'.

Another angle

The coiner of "philosophy", born on Samos around 580 BCE, who fused Orphic spirituality with Presocratic science. In her telling his birth was prophesied at Delphi, he studied for decades in Egypt and Persia, and Iamblichus saw him as an emanation of Apollo. His goal was union with the Monad and his method rests on four pillars; yet he came back to life, married a student, had children who led his school, and trained politicians.

Another angle

The Pythagoreans described the fulfilment of existence as union with the Monad and gave the One the code name Apollo, 'not of the many'. They purified the senses through long silence and living apart, and saw truth as a sphere without circumference. She attributes to Pythagoras 'nothing is random' (flagged uncertain) and finds Pythagorean numbers (the tetractys, the series 1, 4, 7, 10) in the sky.

Roots

Πυθ- (the Pythia, Pythian Apollo) + ἀγορά (marketplace of goods and ideas, ruled by Hermes)

Apollo's voice entering the agora of the many. standard

Cosmos and the One

ἁρμονία

Harmony

harmonía

In Athena’s teaching

Harmony is not the absence of opposites but their sacred union: ἁρμός, a joint, together with κρᾶσις and μῖξις, blending and mixing. With the Pythagoreans she says that without opposition there is no harmony, so we should not fear conflict. Apollo's fourth power, ὁμοπολῶν, moves the poles together into a new unity. In the eros talk, eros is the weft of universal harmony that holds the world in one.

Another angle

Justice is harmony of all levels, and φ is 'the rhythm of harmony': each level relates to every higher one through the same ratio, order and geometry. Establishing justice and harmony in the soul lets it be reflected outside, as above so below.

Another angle

She derives ἁρμονία from ἁρμοί, joints, and ἀραρίσκω, to fit together: the healthy co-existence of everything in the universal polity, like the physicists' unified field where every vibration stands in proportion with all others. Health and harmony spread 'from end to end' of a social whole like organs in a body. Justice is the self-regulating fire that keeps the cosmos in this balance, and in his higher function Ares guards it.

Roots

ἁρμοί (joints) + ἀραρίσκω (to fit together)

Healthy co-existence of all things in proportion. standard

The good life

ἦθος

Ethos and character

êthos

In Athena’s teaching

Ethics does not mean morality: from ἦθος and ἔθος, habit, it is the habitual way the energy of the soul moves, habits of consciousness. Plato's Academy taught it as moulding oneself into a balanced person, and she notes that ἠθική is an anagram of Ἰθάκη, so knowing the structure of the soul is the way home. Its fullest form is the ethics of love, summed up in the teaching that there are no others.

Another angle

Character (ἦθος) comes from habituation (ἔθος), so the lawgiver is not a bureaucrat but a 'character-shaper' (ἠθοπλάστης) whose laws initiate the soul into values; this is why, for her, responsibility lies first with the polity. In the theatre of life the actor, ἠθοποιός, 'makes an ethos' by the way he plays his role. She adds that ἦθος also means τρόπος, which is also the word for a musical mode.

Roots

ἔθος / ἐθισμός (habit / habituation)

Character is formed by habit, so law shapes character. standard

The good life

γενναιότητα

Courageous nobility

gennaiótēta

In Athena’s teaching

Courage is a hinge in two talks. In the Ares lesson the awakened need the courage of the spirited part, a virtue of both warrior and philosopher, or the cave will 'eat' them, and the soul needs fearlessness to cross the passage after death. In the 28 October talk the collective «No» of 1940 was possible only because Greeks had cultivated ἀνδρεία in their souls and were brave in daily life, so their bravery could show on the political level.

Another angle

She calls γενναιότητα, courageous nobility, the opposite of resignation and, in her account of Aristotle, the first moral virtue. Without paideia to keep the soul in it, collective trauma breeds the 'trauma of resignation' she sees in modern Greeks. The Ares archetype makes the same point spiritually: we must be fighters on the path of virtue, and facing one's conscience means 'you must enter the war'.

Another angle

Athena reads ἀνδρεία as ἀντί + ῥέω, going against the current: Socrates says the currents of injustice and illusion in the world are many, and like Theseus, Odysseus or Heracles one must find the strength (σθένος) to swim against them.

Περσεφόνη

Persephone

In Athena’s teaching

In her Eleusinian reading Persephone's three names trace three stages of the soul. As 'bearer of death' (φέρουσα φόνον) she descends and lives the death of truth, identification with the body. As Φερσέφασσα, bearer of light, she carries the light that sets her on the path of gestation and stripping. As Φερέπαφα, bearer of touch, she touches the immortal and returns to Mother Demeter.

Another angle

Like Persephone, the soul descends into Hades, 'and Hades is here', this world of sleep. The initiates come back up resurrected, which is what awakening means.

Soul and mind

αἴσθησις

The senses

aísthēsis

In Athena’s teaching

Against the idea that the spiritual must renounce the senses, she teaches that the philosopher purifies them. Sensation (Timaeus 43a-c) is the moment the river's waves, striking the body, reach the soul's circles; the sense organs are only gates, and it was never the body that sensed but the mind. Rightly understood, the senses are sacred gifts for enjoying God and one of the great initiations of embodied life: we reach fullness not through them but with them as allies.

Another angle

Whoever trusts only what the five senses give still lives in the cave, she says, and seeking the exit through the senses only drives you deeper. Modern education cultivated the five senses and neglected the 'dozens' of the soul's senses, such as intuition, awareness and psychic sight, each a counterpart of a physical sense. As the saying goes, mind sees and mind hears: the soul can withdraw from the organs to turn toward itself.

Another angle

Sight is the 'most sun-like' of the senses, since we see through light, and Plato uses it to lead us from the visible to the intelligible. Opinions about the sensible world sit inside the cave, and liberation includes freedom from the narrow frame in which we interpret the senses.

Roots

ἀΐσσω (to rush, dart)

Sensation as a rushing motion, read through Proclus as motion meeting a still, perceiving position. Athena’s readingReconstructed from unclear captions

Cosmos and the One

εὐοσμία

Smell and aroma

euosmía

In Athena’s teaching

Smell has a special place: it lies between water and air, between sensible and intelligible, and goes straight to memory, so she calls it a direct gate to φρόνησις (which is 'not by chance' akin to ὄσφρησις, smell). Its double nature means a scent can lift the soul (pure flowers, incense, herbs) or drag it down (chemical blends and animal-based perfumes). Incense, θυμίαμα, 'reminds' us (her wordplay) and awakens the soul's Mnemosyne, and whatever we wear and exhale feeds a corresponding order of beings.

The good life

ἀγάπη

Love

In Athena’s teaching

Where eros is the drive toward union, ἀγάπη is the fullness of recognising it. Love is another name for the one, common unity of consciousness, so knowing yourself as love is the single cure for every ill, and love is the beginning of wisdom. Its ethics is concrete: love in word, thought, feeling and act, treating everything as your own household (οἶκος) and doing it selflessly, as Marcus Aurelius taught.

Another angle

The first real mark of awakening is love in its range, fervour and universality: if nothing is separate and all is you, you cannot help loving everything, like a mother, whatever your sex or whether you are a parent. This love is impersonal and holds even where you disagree. In her own life the realisation of oneness brought an equanimity together with equal care for every form of life, with ethical consequences: others' well-being matters as much as your own.

Another angle

What the ancients called cosmic eros we would today call the power of love: the glue holding the universe together. Every relationship, even the political, is erotic by nature. At the end of the path the divine daimon we are is held 'in the embrace of universal love'.

Roots

ἄγω (I lead) + εἰς τὸ ἅπαν (into the All)

Through a Platonic key: love leads into the All, the universe, the harmony of the whole. Ἄγω is active, as in ἡγέτης and παιδαγωγός, so love is not passive. Athena’s reading

κάλλος

In Athena’s teaching

Cosmos and the One

σκότος

Darkness and the descent

skótos

In Athena’s teaching

The winter solstice, the darkest night, is a privileged gate, not a misfortune: darkness means introversion, the time to descend like Persephone into the subconscious with the hero's torch. There you face your monsters, hidden passions and their roots in events, family and ancestors, uproot them and sow virtues. At rock bottom the choice is 'light or nothing', and trauma can become θαῦμα, a miracle.

Another angle

Before arrival, light and darkness seem clearly different; once there, there is no difference. The soul enters dark regions through the passions and loses sight of truth. After the return she says the one in darkness is 'a dream within a dream', and darkness is light very much dimmed.

Ways of knowing

Ἑλληνισμός

Hellenism

Hellēnismós

In Athena’s teaching

Hellenism for her is a universal spirit, not ethnocentric pride, built on two principles: Heraclitus' 'all is one' and 'as above, so below, as within, so without'. Its path was never lost: the golden chain lives in the soul's memory and is allowed again after centuries of bans. In the Pythagoras lesson she tells how a teacher in the Himalayas sent her home: the whole tradition of awakening was already in her own culture.

Another angle

Hellenism is not the era after Alexander but a living worldview and spiritual path, and she prefers "Hellenic" to "Greek". It leans to immanence while holding transcendence, and it offers a secular spirituality without the devotional side of Eastern paths. It is a treasure Greeks are sitting on: a Westerner seeking spirit need not run East, since it is already in this root.

Another angle

Hellenism's distinctive gift, for her, is that science and spirituality are one path: science itself is the way of awakening. She calls the Republic 'the Bible of Hellenism' and traces a lineage from Orpheus (thousands of years ago) through Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle to Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus and Damascius. She links Ἕλλην to the root of spiritual light and calls the holistic Greek worldview a treasury we must return to.

Gods and myths

μῦθος

Myth as symbol

mŷthos

In Athena’s teaching

Myths are theology in the psyche's native symbolic language: mythology is initiation (μύηση) into theology. Homer coded cosmic and karmic laws in analogies, such as Apollo's anger standing for the reaction our actions bring back. Children read such stories literally, which is why Plato filtered tales of jealous or warring gods.

Another angle

Myths are symbols of our own being, not tales of beings 'out there': Zeus is our nous, the Titans are the tensions of becoming, and a hero's parentage tells which circle of the soul he perfected. Ancient texts are likewise gates, not texts: since truth is infinite, the interpretation of an allegory can never be finished.

Soul and mind

κόρος

Desire and fullness

kóros

In Athena’s teaching

Behind every desire that seeks expression through the senses, the soul is seeking the fullness (κόρος) of the Good, so desire is sacred in its motive. Only wrong education makes it believe fullness lies in one more possession or meal, which breeds the ἀκόρεστον, the insatiable, and explains why many wealthy people are unhappy. What we seek outside is already within, reached by the soul's inward turning (μεταστροφή).

Another angle

Material plenty cannot fill us, Athena says, because we are not only body but soul and nous: however much we are paid (πληρωνόμαστε), money cannot fill us (πληρωθούμε). A civilisation that offers no psychic and spiritual food leaves us hungry even with full plates, deprived of knowledge, light, freedom, love, peace, connection and community.

Roots

κόρος (fullness, satiety) + purity (?) (cleanness)

Fullness is linked with purity, and hence with catharsis; its opposite is the insatiable. Athena’s readingReconstructed from unclear captions

Soul and mind

χωριστικότητα

The separate self

chōristikótēta

In Athena’s teaching

Any identity, even 'the awakened one', sets itself against something else and so keeps a gap between the ego and the pure 'I am', between the ego and the One. She lists the false identities in order: I am my role, then my convictions (left, right, Greek, Platonist), then my knowledge (philosopher, scientist, knower), 'again a trap'. Threatened identity is why scholars and scientific communities resist what they do not understand.

Another angle

What falls away in awakening is the belief that you are a separate person, body, soul or mind: in Plotinus' terms not becoming someone else, but 'another' that had wrapped itself around you departing. The separate self is a story, 'a shadow from the cave'. Hence 'an awakened person' is a contradiction, and ego-centred goals (proving yourself, possessions, fame) lose their pull: whom would you be serving?

Another angle

Athena pictures the stream of thoughts as a labyrinth circling the Minotaur, the ego, to whose centre one must go like Theseus. From the start, Athena says, philosophy was a path of love whose aim was to free us from the ego.

Soul and mind

δαίμων

Daimon

daímōn

In Athena’s teaching

Not the Christian demon but the inner true self, a droplet of God and the inner teacher. She derives it from δαίω, I burn, tying it to Heraclitus's ever-living fire, and from a sense of distributing: each daimon is a localised share of the one fire. Eudaimonia is then that flame touching its own good nature.

Another angle

She derives δαίμων from δαήμων, 'one who knows and teaches', and from δαίω, 'I am aflame' (her readings): the daimon is a fiery self-awareness that teaches and reveals because it knows. No one from outside makes you eudaimon; at your core you are this flame of truth. Eudaimonia is known only as daimones and pure minds, never as roles, costumes or personalities.

Another angle

The δαίμων is the inner flame, voice and compass, a spark that never slept, 'the one who knows'. She derives it both from knowing and from δαίω, to burn (cf. δάδα, torch), so touching truth rekindles it. Socrates' daimonion is his inner teacher, the voice of Apollonian consciousness, and εὐδαιμονία is this daimon freed to express the divinity at its core.

Roots

δαήμων (one who knows and teaches) + δαίω (to blaze)

The daimon is a fiery self-awareness that knows and teaches: the flame you are at your core. disputed

Gods and myths

Ζεύς

Zeus

Zeús

In Athena’s teaching

Zeus is consciousness in its creative operation, the cosmic mind. His endless loves and children are not literal: goddesses and mortal women are the divine and ordinary ideas that mind mingles with, and every birth is a world. She reads his two names as two movements, Δίας dividing and projecting, Ζεύς unifying and returning (etymologies she offers as her own).

Another angle

In her reading Zeus is not someone out there but our νοῦς, our awareness: the goat Amalthea nursing infant Zeus is the soul-food released at the Capricorn solstice so that the nous remembers itself. Purified senses can perceive 'the vibration of Zeus', and she reads διάθεσις as 'Διὸς θέσις', the position of Zeus or spirit. She cites the Orphic Hymn to Zeus for a 'liberating witness' that is also a prayer.

Another angle

There is no Apollo without Zeus, the demiurgic nous (after Proclus) that keeps generating ideas and natures, hence his many children. Apollo comes through creation to remind us not to get lost in phenomena but to return to the essence Zeus generates. Talk of Zeus being 'born' is a convention for the human mind: these are simultaneous, qualitative differentiations, not historical events.

Thinkers

Ἀνατολή

Eastern parallels

In Athena’s teaching

She trained in India and found that meditation there cleared her lens until she could read Plato with new eyes: everything was already in her own tradition. She parallels Greek ideas with the Tao, Atman, Buddha nature and yoga, holding that truth is one. Yet the postwar West's turn East met cultural friction, and a message in the Himalayas told her that what she sought was where she started.

Another angle

Having studied Hinduism, Buddhism and Taoism alongside the Greek tradition, she finds the same core under a different 'colour' given by culture, history and place. Those who realise awakening in any tradition live the same state. She draws on the Buddhist luminous void and calls philosophy, anachronistically, 'the yoga of the Greeks'.

Another angle

She draws parallels with India and Tibet: Plotinus' ἕνωσις is what others call yoga, the Greek teacher dedicated to all beings mirrors the bodhisattva, and the Buddha's 'the right moment is now' matches the Greek νῦν. She links the divisions of the Circle of the Other to the seven chakras, and Autobiography of a Yogi turned her own life toward meditation in 2008.

The path

θέασις

Beholding (theasis)

théasis

In Athena’s teaching

θέασις, beholding, is how she says the Greek tradition names awakening: 'the beholding of the One', in which often nothing happens, no gate opens, no angel appears; you simply witness what already is. It shares a root with θέατρον and θεατής: we come into the divine theatre as spectators of truth. Her formula from the Republic is that a change of θέασις (seeing) leads to θέωσις (deification).

Another angle

She says the ancient word for awakening is θέασις, beholding, not something that happens to you. Θέα and θέωσις contain θεός and θεά: to behold is to see what is already here waiting for you, what you are. Truth does not come to you; you come to it, and what shifts is the vision (μετατόπιση θέας), not the world.

Another angle

For her θέασις is the ancient name for what we now call awakening: reaching the beholding of the Good, or touching truth. It is called beholding precisely because nothing is created and nothing happens; only a pure seeing arises. With Plotinus she says this seeing turns out to be union: there were not two.

The path

ἀποφατική

The apophatic way

apophatikḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Because what is realised is ἄρρητον, belonging neither to words nor concepts, she begins by saying what awakening is not: apophatic theology or knowledge. Diotima does the same with absolute beauty (no body, no limbs, no colour). Her practical test follows: while you still see or understand 'something', even God or the light, do not stop; you have not reached Ithaca.

Another angle

She defines awakening largely by what it is not: not a political revelation, not an out-of-body or energy experience, not small tastes. The Good is beyond knowledge and truth, ineffable, so whoever insists on knowing it is stuck at an earlier stage: one must let knowledge go to dive into the source.

The path

ἀνάμνησις

Recollection (anamnesis)

anámnēsis

In Athena’s teaching

All knowledge is recollection because the soul's essence is the essence of the cosmos and the divine: knowing is not shopping for something new but activating an imprint already within. Feeling a lack proves it, as you cannot look for keys you do not know you lost. Activating the soul's memory (μνημοσύνη) is, for the ancients, activating eudaimonia; incense 'reminds' us, and her own first reading of Plato at 14 felt like remembering.

Another angle

With Plato she holds that all knowledge is recollection. Like an olive seed carrying the tree's genetic material, we carry 'psychic genetic material': the seeds of eudaimonia, knowledge and freedom, forgotten but never lost. In the Pythagoras lesson the path itself is stored in the soul's μνημοσύνη in the heart, and the name of Pythagoras' father, Mnesarchus, means memory ruling.

Another angle

Plato says knowledge is recollection, so teaching means reminding: activating the innate power of ἰδεῖν rather than inserting knowledge. Following Plotinus, she adds that whoever comes into union with the One was always the One and simply remembered it.

Cosmos and the One

ταὐτόν / θάτερον

The Circles of the Same and the Other

tautón / tháteron

In Athena’s teaching

From the Timaeus and Proclus she teaches that the soul is two circular strips joined in a χ. The Circle of the Same, matching the celestial equator, is the Hestia within that keeps us centred in being; the Circle of the Other, matching the ecliptic and zodiac and divided into seven (she links these to the chakras and planets), carries senses, passions and changing moods. θάτερον is an anagram of θέατρον, the theatre of roles. True human life is their conscious union; equinox and solstice mark their meeting and their greatest distance.

The good life

φρόνησις

Phronesis (practical wisdom)

phrónēsis

In Athena’s teaching

She gives φρόνησις the etymology 'φορᾶς καὶ ῥοῦ νόησις', understanding of motion and flow, the right circular motion of the mind. How far we reach it depends on how we use the senses, on finding the 'algorithm of relationship' between the river's motions and the soul's. Calm (γαλήνη) lets the circles recover so judgment becomes correct, and smell (ὄσφρησις) is 'not by chance' its kin.

Roots

φορά (motion, carrying) + ῥοῦς / ῥοή (flow) + νόησις (understanding)

Practical wisdom is understanding of motion and flow, the right circular motion of nous; 'not by chance' akin to ὄσφρησις, smell. disputed

Cosmos and the One

Matter

In Athena’s teaching

Matter does not exist apart from consciousness: in the Platonic tradition it is an emanation (ἀπορροή), the last stage of the One's outflowing light, and 'the universe is noetic'. She calls matter-as-primary 'the biggest fake news', an interpretation of consciousness seen at a tilt. Still, the material world is no prison: a provident Demiurge made it as a sacred play of consciousness, and physicists' 'energy soup' is better called an 'energy river'.

Cosmos and the One

αἰών

Eternity and time

aiṓn

In Athena’s teaching

Following Plato, time is the moving image of eternity, while eternity itself does not move except around itself, like the sun, a sphere or the spinning top of Dionysus. She reads χρόνος as χ (duality) + ῥοή (flow) + νοῦς, from a source the notes cannot identify. In the noetic there is no time; past is memory and future projection. Plotinus' eternity is untrembling (ἀτρεμής), untilted (ἀκλινής) and 'standing in the one'.

Roots

ἀεί (always) + ὤν (being)

Aion is 'that which always is', the playing child within us. Athena’s reading

The path

τέλος / ἐντελέχεια

Telos and entelechy

télos / entelécheia

In Athena’s teaching

The Greek universe is teleological: nothing is random, and everything tends dynamically toward its purpose, a force that constantly pulls us. Perfection (τελειότητα) is not an abstract ideal but the fulfilment of one's τέλος. Like a seed carrying the whole oak, the soul tends toward eudaimonia because it comes from eudaimonia: our origin is our Ithaca.

Another angle

Diotima teaches that the goal of eros coincides with the goal of human life: the reason we incarnated, the goal of all goals, the reason we do anything at all. That goal is to remind us of the pure divine nature we already are. Steering eros rightly lets it lead where nature set it to lead.

The path

ἀπορία

Aporia (not-knowing)

aporía

In Athena’s teaching

If I do not recognise that I do not know, I do not ask. Admitting not-knowing, Socrates' method, opens the pores (ἀπορία), and then Apollo starts to reveal himself. This is the restlessness of the first step, Pythios, together with the natural appetite (ὀρέγεσθαι) for knowledge that Aristotle describes.

Another angle

The path begins by forgetting what we think we know, like Socrates' 'I know that I know nothing'. She reads aporia as opening the soul's 'pores' by admitting 'I do not know'. Truth is a Heraclitean flow, not a thing to capture and raise as a banner: whoever claims to hold it as 'something' has lost it.

Roots

ἀ- (without) + πόρος (passage, pore)

Admitting 'I do not know' opens the soul's pores. Athena’s reading

The path

κάθαρσις

Purification

kátharsis

In Athena’s teaching

Purification runs through her teaching: cathartic virtues (diet, mantras, energy work, cleansing the luminous body that the Chaldean Oracles call the soul's subtle vehicle), Epimenides lifting karma from cities, Diotima cleansing the plague's residue, and tragedy purging audiences through imitation of heroes' passions. Such energetic cleansing, she stresses, is not only an Eastern or New Age idea but is in the Hellenic sources.

Another angle

The philosopher's task in the Republic is to purify the senses, not renounce them: purified senses perceive 'the vibration of Zeus' and attune us to the One. Eudaimonia is a process of stripping (ἀπογύμνωσις) false beliefs, passions and self-images until one is a 'naked soul'. Pure aromas, flowers and incense cleanse and raise the aura, and simply facing your shadows with the wish for transformation begins the alchemy.

Another angle

Apollo's first etymology, ἀπολούων, means washing: cleansing what we thought we knew, the views, poles and habits (ἕξεις) that cause suffering and war. Awakening is the lifting of veils as we clean, until clarity appears. Apollo also 'destroys' (ἀπόλλυμι), but only the useless, a good loss; and the Python's stagnant waters must flow for the soul's oracle to be cleansed.

Cosmos and the One

παίγνιον

Life as divine play

paígnion

In Athena’s teaching

She calls the phenomenal world a δρώμενον, a sacred enactment, staged within the mind of God, who imagines or dreams it; in this sense it is a phantasm, at once collective and individual. Following Proclus, essence falls into a 'divine sleep' and dreams the many, and death ends the dream. These are her metaphysical views. Practically, the awakened watch the shadow play (she compares it to Karagiozis) while remembering 'I am not this'.

Another angle

The second mark of awakening is εὐθυμία, a childlike cheer that comes from seeing life as Dionysus' divine theatre, where the One plays every role and we are spectators of truth. Heraclitus' Aeon is a child playing dice, the dice being the One's possibilities. You may still have to play a role, even a strict or serious one, but you play it without becoming it.

The path

κοσμοθέασις

Worldview (kosmotheasis)

kosmothéasis

In Athena’s teaching

She frames whole talks around worldview: the dualist one that splits spirit from matter and humans from nature, and the holistic, unitive Greek one in which sensible and intelligible form a single continuum. Worldview is not academic: she reads the state of the planet as the fruit of a mistaken worldview, and estrangement from natural rhythm as the reason humanity destroys its environment and itself.

The good life

μεσότης

Measure and the mean

mesótēs

In Athena’s teaching

The soul's circles run on the mathematical measure that the geometer-God gave them, the ratios of the Timaeus, and violent contact with the river can make them lose it. The centre, the mean (μεσότης), is the hearth of virtue, divine nature and eudaimonia. So she advises not to complain about moderate circumstances: they make the inner equinox, the meeting of the two circles, easier.

The path

ΕΙ / εἶ

The Delphic E

ei

In Athena’s teaching

The cryptic letter E at Delphi, which she attributes, with "Know thyself", to Apollo himself. Of the many readings Plutarch discusses she favours εἶ, "you are", the second person of "I am". Placed beside the precept, it tells the pilgrim that the divinity sought in the temple and in things is what the pilgrim already is.

Another angle

She reads the Delphic E as the number 5, the unmoving centre of the cosmic balance: among the numbers 1 to 9, five stands in the middle. She cites Iamblichus' cosmic seesaw of numbers, with 5 at the centre as justice, heart and providence.

Athena connects it to

    It names the true self as the divine

  • Plutarch

    Plutarch wrote On the E at Delphi.

  • Justice

    Five at the centre is justice.

Gods and myths

Ἀθηνᾶ

Athena (the goddess)

Athēnâ

In Athena’s teaching

In the Ares lesson Athena is war 'by union': through providence and strategy she removes the monstrous and passionate so that beings reunite, using every other means before bloody war, and she always overpowers Ares because wisdom rules force. In the radio interview she names wisdom as the goddess's first virtue, joined by justice, temperance and discernment. Her birth from Zeus's head means wisdom is the fruiting (κάρπισμα) of mind, its τέλος.

Another angle

In the Odyssey the goddess is the divine guide who brings the lost soul home to Ithaca. She stands for philosophy, science, knowledge and virtue, and Potari calls her ἠθονόη, the one who knows the characters (ἤθη). Working with her means ethics, self-knowledge and a fresh, serious study of one's own tradition.

Another angle

Her symbol, the owl (γλαύξ), can turn its head and so has all-round, overseeing (ἐποπτική) vision: the opposite of the chained prisoners' one-sidedness.

The good life

φιλότης

Philotes, cosmic love

philótēs

In Athena’s teaching

The Presocratic, above all Empedoclean, name for the cohesive, attractive force that makes the many into one universe; Empedocles said everything is ruled by attraction and repulsion, as physics now says too. To know ourselves as cosmic φιλότης is, for her, the panacea for separateness. Self-knowledge leads to it, and from it comes the Neoplatonic call to love all things.

Another angle

Pythagoras defined philosophy as φιλότης toward wisdom, so the path begins by cultivating the art of loving, the purified heart. In the Ares lesson the Presocratics' two cosmic forces are Νεῖκος, strife or division, and Φιλότης, love or union: both are divine workers in the architecture of the cosmos, embodied by Ares and Athena.

Another angle

The word philo-sophia says what must be activated first: φιλότης, love, cultivated together with consciousness until one remembers the One. Her second closing practice is φιλότης: training in love and kindness towards oneself and all beings. Love for all beings and for the common good is, for Plato, the precondition of politics.

The good life

ἰδιώτης

The idiotes

idiṓtēs

In Athena’s teaching

In ancient Greece whoever cut himself off from the whole ('what do I care what society does') was an ἰδιώτης, and English kept the word as 'idiot'. She reads ἠλίθιος not as an insult but as a cognitive state: one who lives 'in lethe', having forgotten he is one with his fellow citizens and with everything. He sees himself as a little seashell in the ocean of the absolute, and she calls this a personal and collective disease of Greek society.

Another angle

In ancient Greece the private person concerned only with his own interest was a negative figure who loses his human worth, his life spinning around ego and private affairs like an angular momentum (στροφορμή). English borrowed the word as "idiot" for good reason: failing to see that you are first a collective being is a kind of damage. Loving another person is the first step out of this state.

Another angle

She contrasts the ἰδιώτης, the private person living 'for my own sake', with the πολίτης and κοσμοπολίτης of the last steps. Instead of waking up asking what to do for one's own little circle, one acts for the whole. She asks how much we do each day only to maintain an imaginary persona.

Roots

ἴδιος (one's own, private)

The private, self-serving person; English 'idiot' later took the sense of one asleep in λήθη. standard

Cosmos and the One

ἐντελέχεια

Entelechy

entelécheia

In Athena’s teaching

She glosses Aristotle's word as the τέλος we have (ἔχειν) within (ἐν). As an olive seed carries the blossoming, fruiting olive tree, the soul carries the end for which it incarnated, and that end is εὐδαιμονία. In the 28 October talk the human entelechy is to attune one's existence to the Good, and she uses it against the social-contract view: our inner end is goodness, not wickedness.

Another angle

Aristotle's word, read as ἐν (inside), τέλος (end) and ἔχειν (to have): the end we carry within, our inner ontological programme. As the acorn holds the oak, or Demeter's wheat seed its plant, the human being carries the telos of lasting happiness and realises it when conditions allow, bringing the inner fountain into life as creativity.

Roots

ἐν (inside) + τέλος (end, perfection) + ἔχειν (to have)

We carry our purpose inside, as the acorn carries the oak. standard

Ways of knowing

γνῶσις

Gnosis

In Athena’s teaching

One of the four names of philosophy's goal: non-dual awareness that rises beyond phenomena and duality to realise what is already whole and divine. It is freedom-giving knowledge, and she calls the final stage of Hellenic meditation, where subject and object merge, the very meaning of gnosis.

Another angle

On the Line, knowledge of concepts and then of numbers lies above the cave, 'almost there'. But the Good is 'after knowledge': at the top of the line knowledge ends in union, and the identity 'I the knower' is another trap.

Hellenic meditation

In Athena’s teaching

She presents a native Greek meditation path, not borrowed yoga: focused contemplation (στοχασμός), expansive inner dialogue of awareness (διαλογισμός), then non-dual gazing. Gods and myths

σύμβολον

Symbol and archetype

sýmbolon

In Athena’s teaching

A symbol carries something sensible (a king sailing to Troy and back) up to the intelligible level of the laws of human and cosmic nature. Jung's archetype is, in her view, a renaming of this Greek idea. Tragedy proves the point, since only living archetypes could produce catharsis; and for Greeks the Odyssey is a symbol, while Hollywood treats it as merchandise.

Another angle

Awakening, like number, cannot be pointed at: 'two' appears in endless sensible forms yet is one idea, and the noetic cannot be reduced to the sensible. So the ancients call it ἄρρητον, unspeakable, and use symbols, which are ἀναβαθμοί, steps leading up from the sensible. Proclus adds that every word is a seed that ripens into realisation.

Thinkers

Ὅμηρος

Homer

Hómēros

In Athena’s teaching

The Homeric epics were the pillars of Greekness and the source of tragedy's archetypes; Homer may even be the title of a rhapsode rather than one person. Plato gave a whole book of the Republic to Homer and filtered his literal-sounding stories, since Homer coded cosmic laws in analogies. Healing, for Greeks, means bending over Homer's spring again to drink the water of Mnemosyne.

Gods and myths

Ἰθάκη / νόστος

Ithaca and nostos

Ithákē / nóstos

In Athena’s teaching

Νόστος, Odysseus' sweet homecoming, is what gives life its νοστιμιά, its flavour, and its eudaimonia. Yet arrival is not completion: Odysseus reaches Ithaca only mid-Odyssey and must still face the suitors, which she tentatively reads as our illusions, just as the freed prisoner returns to the cave. In the 28 October talk Ἰθάκη is an anagram of ἠθική: the passions toss us on stormy seas and make us lose our Ithaca, so coming home is ethics. With Cavafy, we meet the monsters on the way only if we carry them in our soul.

Another angle

Ithaca is the inner centre: fullness, freedom and eudaimonia, and νόστος, homecoming, means returning to what one loves. The goddess leads Odysseus not to a new continent but back to where he began, now changed and occupied by suitors. Her wordplay that ἠθική is an anagram of Ἰθάκη makes ethics the road home, and she stresses that return means renewal, not nostalgia.

Another angle

Odysseus leaves Ithaca for the war of the many and must return; we too have fought long for the νόστιμον ἦμαρ, the day of return, which is eudaimonia, our home. She matches the journey to the Neoplatonic procession, remaining and return.

Thinkers

Πολιτεία

Plato's Republic

Politeía

In Athena’s teaching

She calls it Plato's magnum opus: if all his other works were lost, its quintessence would survive in it. Subtitled 'On the Just', it begins in Piraeus with the question of justice and covers soul, virtues, constitutions, music, education, epistemology and life after death. It must be read whole, not in excerpts, and its core thesis is that the just city cannot exist outside unless it is first built in the soul.

Another angle

She teaches the Republic almost every year, calls it the Bible of philosophy and an ark of knowledge, and wrote her LSE dissertation on it as an initiation. It presents a vision of realising the One through social and political structures, and its treatment of music and Homer is regulation, not banishment. Her course Building the Republic within and without reads the healthy city as a model for a healthy character, from which outer change follows.

Cosmos and the One

The golden thread and its cut

In Athena’s teaching

She traces one lineage from Orpheus (an avatar and son of the Muses who founded the mysteries) through the Presocratics, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, the Stoics and the Neoplatonists, ended when Justinian closed the schools in 529 AD on pain of death. The church kept the logic, cosmology and ethics but erased the practices, leaving a dissected corpus of texts without methods. The spirit went underground and, she says, is now being rekindled in Greece as an indigenous path.

Ways of knowing

πνευματικότητα

Spirituality and religion

In Athena’s teaching

She warns that spiritual people have been trained to be 'lukewarm water', soft and guilty about strength, and calls this a cave strategy to disarm awakening. Strong traditions (Greek, Hindu, Tibetan, Native American) pair the illuminated one with the warrior, and only declining traditions undermine the warrior. The more refined we are inside, the firmer we must be outside, and spiritual work is incomplete until it becomes action and life.

Another angle

She hesitates over the word because of its religious ring: what Hellenism offers is a secular path into spirit without devotional aspects. Religion is organised spirituality that often loses its spirit and becomes politicised, as the Tao Te Ching says when the Tao is lost religion appears. Theological in the Greek sense does not mean religious, and calling philosophy mystical is unnecessary because that was its original meaning.

Another angle

The Age of Aquarius brings both more searching for truth and unfiltered ideas: awakening as visions, beings from other stars, a body emitting light, walking on water. She calls this confusing the phenomenon with the essence. Signs and synchronicities belong to the second step, but the task is to stabilise them into a way of life, not to chase them.

Cosmos and the One

θεῖον / θέωσις

The divine and the gods

theîon / théōsis

In Athena’s teaching

There are three ways to approach any god, text or idea, all true at once: external, at the πρόναος ('I am here, Apollo is there'); internal, Orphic, where the god becomes a power of my soul; and central, mysteriac, where the god is lived as an active mode of being of the One. The god appears differently according to the seeker's tuning. θέασις contains θεός and θεά, so beholding is meeting the divine that is already here.

Another angle

The gods are operations, energies and movements of the ineffable One, symbolised by the whole pantheon and decoded by Platonic commentators. The divine is immanent, in everything and everyone, and one purpose of philosophy is θέωσις, realising our own divine being. The Presocratics saw matter itself as animate and woven with the divine.

Another angle

For the ancients, Athena says, God was the alpha and omega of philosophy: there was no philosophy without God. At the summit one no longer believes in God or the Good but witnesses and lives it.

Ways of knowing

ἑλληνικὴ γλῶσσα

The Greek language

hellēnikḕ glôssa

In Athena’s teaching

Greek is a performative, vibratory language: like Beethoven or a mantra it cannot truly be translated, and reading it in the original acts on soul and energy. Following the Cratylus and Proclus she holds that letters and words encode movements of being, so a teaching can be drawn out of a single word. Her talks are full of such indigenous etymologies, which she admits grammarians may contest.

Another angle

Athena speaks 'with the Greek codes', because the language encodes concepts and helps us philosophise: κοινότητα holds κοινό, σκοτώνω holds σκότος. Athena urges learning Greek from the ancient sources rather than from its European interpreters, beginning with Plato's Cratylus, whose etymological keys have little to do with today's prevailing linguistics.

Ways of knowing

μουσική / Μοῦσαι

Music and the Muses

mousikḗ / Moûsai

In Athena’s teaching

Music is Apollo's fourth power and, for her, the art of harmonising opposites rather than playing an instrument. Socrates' daimonion told him 'make music and work at it', which she reads as reaching the last Apollonian step: having gone beyond the poles, return to the many and harmonise them. Like the freed prisoner going back into the cave, the philosopher must make music with others, which she calls the political step of consciousness. The aim is a stable, virtuous, 'musical' life.

Another angle

She reads the command Socrates received in the Phaedo, 'make music', as the whole Pythagorean programme. Every psychic power is a frequency, every frequency a ratio of two numbers, so the soul is numbers dancing, and to make music is to tune the soul's inner arrangement by the laws of good order and rhythm, which in human terms are the virtues. That harmony becomes a gate to the One, and the words 'and work' send the realised one back to embody it in the world.

Another angle

Music, meaning all the arts of the Muses, is to the soul what exercise is to the body, and political change begins with the musical modes a society listens to. Because ἦθος is crystallised vibration, Plato placed music under the lawgiver's care rather than banishing the poets. Listening is, she says, the most important spiritual act, and the Muses are doorways to essence.

The good life

ψυχοπολιτική

Psycho-politics

psychopolitikḗ

In Athena’s teaching

Political regimes, she argues, match the psychic state of the people. When the desiring part (ἐπιθυμητικόν), fed by consumerism and advertising, seizes the reins from the heart's beat for freedom and the capacity for knowledge, a people gets an 'oligarchic tyranny' that calls itself democracy. So the first polity to govern is one's own soul: without self-mastery, from what position would you govern others?

Another angle

From Plato she takes the idea that the soul comes first and generates constitutions. Hence her term psycho-political trauma: modern Greece, lacking smooth historical continuity and a settled identity, carries an unhealed wound, so when Hollywood treats a sacred symbol as merchandise (her cultural colonialism) the reaction is psychic, not racist. Healing the soul precedes political change.

Another angle

People once said that to diagnose a polity you should look at its arts; she proposes looking at how its citizens approach eros: from which energy centre, with what vision, from what consciousness. As we approach eros, so we approach our collective union, which is also erotic. She suggests research into which kinds of eros different regimes and societies promote.

The path

ἄγνοια / χωριστικότητα

Ignorance as separateness

ágnoia / chōristikótēta

In Athena’s teaching

The prisoners' defining mark is double ignorance: they do not know that they do not know, and take the cave for life itself. Worse still is to believe you know. Such people call the spiritual seeker mad and later persecute those who return to free them; Plato defines paideia against ἀμάθεια, the state of not-learning.

Another angle

The single root of every evil, personal, political and planetary, is ignorance, specifically χωριστικότητα, the illusion that I am separate from others, from other nations and from nature. It is the same weed behind violence, war and ecological ruin. One disease means one panacea: knowing ourselves as love.

Ways of knowing

κρίσις

Crisis

krísis

In Athena’s teaching

Eras of crisis, she says, have always been more fertile for conceiving the seed of change: transformations follow a crisis. In the radio interview she reads the pandemic, harsh as it was, as a 'blessing' that forced the turning inward on everyone at once, as if life itself made us practise asceticism together and ask where the basis of our well-being lies. These are her interpretations of the crisis, offered as a spiritual reading. In the 28 October talk she warns that a force for change with no rooted values is soon swallowed by the old system.

Another angle

A crisis is a cut (τομή) between how things were and how they will be, and in that cut new ideas hatch; spiritual renaissances are always cradled in crisis. That is why she sees crisis-hit Greece at the threshold of a spiritual renaissance. Covid likewise exposed the betrayal of external foundations and turned people inward.

Fence of Olympus

In Athena’s teaching

Her favourite line of the hymn calls Ares the ἕρκος Ὀλύμπου, the fence or fortress of Olympus. She pictures him as the line of shields around the gods and as the outer electron shell around Hestia's nucleus: the outermost layer is the most exposed, which is why the myths show him straying and switching sides. Spiritually it means our centre is wisdom but our edges must be red, because creation, the soul and awakening all need guarded boundaries; she also links ὅρκος, the oath, to setting a boundary.

The path

μελέτη θανάτου

Practice of death

melétē thanátou

In Athena’s teaching

Her second definition of philosophy comes from the Phaedo: the philosopher accomplishes in life what fate accomplishes for everyone at death, the release of the soul from the body. She stresses that this means dis-identifying from the body, not leaving it, and that touching truth and dying are the same thing. She often quotes a modern teacher: if you die before you die, you will not die when you die.

  • Second birth of the soul

Gods and myths

Ὀρφεύς

Orpheus

Orpheús

In Athena’s teaching

In the Ares lesson Orpheus is the author of the hymn cycle, and the order of its last five hymns is itself a teaching. In the Pythagoras lesson she reads ΟΡΦΕΑΣ as an anagram of ΦΟΡΕΑΣ, the carrier of the flowing light, a first 'avatar' bearing Athena's primordial wisdom. The Orphic current is the heart-centred, ecstatic, Dionysian way that had degenerated by Pythagoras' time and that he reformed, and the Orphic teachers place the soul's memory in the ἦτορ, the spiritual heart.

Another angle

The Orphics teach the internal approach to the gods: still dual, but the god becomes a power of my soul, and the task is to become Apollonian.

The path

ὁ νοῶν

Know the knower

ho noôn

In Athena’s teaching

Her deepest reading of self-knowledge is to turn consciousness back on itself and ask who the one who knows is. You find no someone and no something, only boundlessness (ἀπεραντοσύνη), freedom, timelessness, calm and peace. This consciousness is the stable basis of every experience, pure knowing that knows itself and that, through its modifications, made the appearance of the many. She calls it easy, a meditation one can do now and repeat.

The path

αποταύτιση

Dis-identification

apotáftisi

In Athena’s teaching

Her own word for the Platonic separation of soul from body is αποταύτιση, dis-identification: not leaving the body but ceasing to take it for oneself. You have a body, emotions, desires and thoughts that change from age five to a hundred, while the 'I am' stays. Its fruit is freedom from the illusion of a self bounded by the skin, and in the radio interview it appears as undressing the roles and labels (name, profession, parent, nationality) that cripple the divine self.

Another angle

In the Vox interview Athena lists what we take for the self: thoughts, which pass while I remain; emotions that turn from sorrow to joy; desires; our parents' 'musts'; the image we want to show. All of it is the non-self, and the light of intellect must pierce these layers to reach the protagonist at the centre.

The path

ἀφαίρεσις

Truth by subtraction

aphaíresis

In Athena’s teaching

Truth, for her, is a subtractive process. You need to acquire nothing, because the soul already carries the seeds of eudaimonia, knowledge and freedom and is 'baptised in the light of wisdom'; you only remove what covers it. On the radio she pictures it as a flower opening petal by petal as we shed roles. In the 28 October talk every subtraction is a «No», which is why the national «No» stirs Greeks, though a «No» must then be completed by a «Yes».

Another angle

Asked what self-knowledge made Athena cast off, the answer is 'everything': ways of living, diet, habits, identities, labels and roles, since one in love with truth, like any lover, will do everything. And when every title, role and expectation is gone, what remains is everything: the All.

    What we subtract are false identities

  • Recollection (anamnesis)

    We remove what hides what we already know

  • Truth

    Truth is reached by removing, not adding

  • The One

    When everything is taken away, the All (ἅπαν) remains.

Ways of knowing

ἀλήθεια

Aletheia, unforgetting

alḗtheia

In Athena’s teaching

She reads ἀλήθεια as alpha privative plus λήθη: truth is the lifting of forgetfulness. This fits Plato's teaching that knowledge is recollection, so knowing is activating what we already carry, not conquering something foreign, which she calls one of the most distinctive features of the Greek view. In the Pythagoras lesson she adds an anagram: ἀλήθεια and θήλεια, the female, so truth is always gestating and giving birth.

The path

ἐφάπτεσθαι / ἅπτω

Touching truth

In Athena’s teaching

For the ancients, she says, philosophy's goal was to touch (ἐφάπτεσθαι) the truth experientially, not to master arguments. The touch is as tangible as touch, the heaviest sense, yet as dimensionless as Euclid's point. Since ἅπτω also means to kindle (think of a lighter, αναπτήρας), touching truth sets the whole being ablaze and rekindles the inner fire, contact with Heraclitus' ever-living fire.

The path

ἕνωσις

Union with the Monad

hénōsis

In Athena’s teaching

Ἕνωσις with the Monad is Pythagoras' name for what others call yoga, 'union', or nirvana, and for her it is the aim of philosophy. It is not reaching something far away but realising, with mind, heart and body, that you and the cosmic ocean are already one. The final step of the Pythagorean school, ὁμοίωσις θεῷ, is the same awakening: my essence and the universe's essence are one.

Another angle

With Plotinus, Socrates and the Presocratics Athena names ἕνωσις as the aim, and stresses that union is not noetic like knowledge: to know, a subject must stand before an object, while in union that division collapses. Hence Plotinus' line that the seer was one with the seen, 'not a vision but a union', and why the ancients called it mystery.

    There one no longer believes but witnesses.

The good life

ἔργον

Work and action

In Athena’s teaching

Awakening must become work. After 'make music' comes 'and work': like the freed prisoner who goes back down, the realised one builds the insight into a way of life, which is why the highest Pythagorean initiation was political. She glosses ἔργον as ἔρωτος γόνος, offspring of eros. In the Ares lesson all work and industriousness run on Arean energy, 'the moment I stand up', and truth not expressed in action is incomplete truth.

Ἕλλην

What is a Hellene

In Athena’s teaching

For her 'Hellene' is a level of the soul, not an ethnicity or a seed asleep in the DNA: an existential, cultural and spiritual achievement. She reads the name through 'Ἑλ', which she takes as spiritual light, so a Hellene is one who tunes his mind to that light, and since light knows no borders a Hellene cannot look after his own interest alone. Many Greeks, she says, are Hellenes in potential (ἐν δυνάμει) but not in actuality (ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ); in 1940 they were Hellenes in actuality.

She reads the «No» of 28 October 1940 as a philosophical lesson. Every subtraction on the path is a «No», said first within, which is why the national «No» stirs every Greek. As above, so below

In Athena’s teaching

The second principle of Hellenism in her 28 October talk: what is above is like what is below, and what is within is like what is without, so there is continuity across all scales. She says it was in a sense given by the Greeks to the Egyptians and engraved on an emerald tablet, which she offers as her account. In Plato it becomes the mirroring of soul and polity, and in the Ares lesson the same law makes the force behind outer law a model for the soul.

The good life

πολιτικὸς ἔρως

Political eros

politikòs érōs

In Athena’s teaching

Against the modern foundation of politics on fear, she proposes the ancient one: political eros. It carries a positive sign of hope and love, and it is the summit of Diotima's ascent, an eros that rises beyond a beautiful body and soul to embrace the whole city: its nature, trees, buildings, citizens, institutions and laws. Since eros is activated by the καλόν, we must make ourselves lovable: be the change.

In Athena’s teaching

The word 'cultivation' is used for only two human activities, she notes: tilling the earth and tending the soul, so soul and earth are strangely identified. The three parts of the soul

In Athena’s teaching

She uses Plato's three parts of the soul in four talks: the desiring part, the spirited part, which she equates with the heart and emotions, and the reasoning part. Studying them is the first, valid stage of self-knowledge and an 'extremely therapeutic' practice of observation. But they are powers of the soul, not the soul: as the melody is not the kithara, the maker is not the made. Politically, when desire takes the reins, a people's regime turns tyrannical.

Soul and mind

ἀποδοχή / ἔστω

Acceptance and the ἔστω

apodochḗ / éstō

In Athena’s teaching

For hard times she offers a mathematician's tool. As a proof starts from 'ἔστω', 'let it be so', one can take as a working hypothesis that everything is perfect and just and must happen for some reason, since from partway up the mountain we cannot see all the folds. Saying 'let it be' is acceptance, an attitude of mind and heart; because the ego is a form of resistance, each acceptance opens us to the Whole.

Another angle

In the Vox interview Athena separates acceptance from tolerance and from resignation. Accepting while boiling inside is not acceptance: ἀποδοχή holds δέχομαι, to receive, to make room, and to forgive (συγχωρώ) and give something room near you is already love. To accept is to light a thing with understanding, to put oneself in the other's place and to embrace it with love; then, no longer entangled, one has the strength to act with discernment, even to leave. Fighting something keeps it close, as Ares and Aphrodite are a couple.

    Accepting and letting go

  • The Golden Verses

    Bear what fate brings without indignation

  • Love

    Making room for something, even forgiving it, is already love.

  • Ares

    Fighting what we do not accept keeps us entangled in it.

μαντική

Mantic knowing

In Athena’s teaching

Μαντική for her is not laurel-chewing or tripods but unmediated knowledge, reached in inner silence rather than by reading, being told or proving. It comes from divine μανία, which she reads as the sacred marriage of heart and nous, not madness. It is Apollo's second power (ἁπλοῦς): removing the many judgements reveals a simple truth, and 'each of us is a seer'. The great ideas of Einstein, Planck, Heisenberg and Tesla came this way, in flashes, with proofs later.

Thinkers

Πλούταρχος

Plutarch

Ploútarchos

In Athena’s teaching

In On the E at Delphi Plutarch gives the five cult names of Apollo, learned from his teacher Ammonius, each matched to the seeker's condition; she reads them as five steps of awakening. He also treats Apollo and Dionysus as one, two states of the universe: the One becoming many and the many returning in a luminous, non-material fire. She departs from him in one place: he groups Delios and Phanaios together, while she makes them two separate steps.

Another angle

Plutarch, philosopher and priest at Delphi, is Athena's witness that 'know thyself' was not given by a human but by Apollo himself, the light itself, which is why it was written on his temple as the god's own precept.

Athena connects it to

  • Apollo

    He supplies the five cult names.

  • Dionysus

    He treats Dionysus and Apollo as one.

  • The Delphic E

  • Delphi

    His five names belong to the Delphic god.

  • Plato's Cratylus

    His five names and the Cratylus' four make nine keys.

  • Know thyself

    As priest of Delphi he says Apollo gave the maxim.

Thinkers

Κρατύλος

Plato's Cratylus

Kratýlos

In Athena’s teaching

In the Cratylus Socrates gives four etymologies of Apollo's name matching his four powers: medicine (ἀπολούων), mantic (ἁπλοῦς), archery (ἀεὶ βάλλων) and music (ὁμοπολῶν). She uses them as the four passages between Plutarch's five names, since five steps have four intervals. She also takes from it the principle that letters can interchange and similar words share meaning, which licenses her wordplay.

Another angle

Athena thinks everyone should read the Cratylus, because it gives the etymological keys of Greek, keys that have little or nothing to do with today's prevailing linguistics. To define love Athena uses 'a Platonic key': ἀγάπη from ἄγω and ἅπαν.

Athena connects it to

  • Plato

    A Platonic dialogue.

  • Socrates

    Socrates gives the etymologies.

  • The ennead

    Its four complete the nine.

  • The Greek language

    Similar words share meaning.

ὑγίεια / ῥῶσις

Health and healing

In Athena’s teaching

Apollo's first power is healing: father of Asclepius, he heals through light and pure vision. Greek medicine is holistic, illness starting in spirit or nous, then soul, then body; illness is complication and health is simplicity and a mean, with the noetic idea as the stable centre. In the eros talk, living in the flow of eros gives ῥῶσις, vigour, and with Socrates health is inner peace while illness is an inner civil war. Healing begins with the will to change.

The path

γραμμή

The divided line

grammḗ

In Athena’s teaching

She reads the Line as the ordering of what the Sun taught: five objects of seeing or thinking and five modes of consciousness, from conjecture and opinion inside the cave, through knowledge of concepts and of numbers above it, to union with the Good at its top. She stresses that she decodes these five from the text rather than adding them, and that they match Plato's five levels of being, the five constitutions and the Pythagorean pentagram. The line is drawn in the mean and extreme ratio, φ.

δόξα / πεποίθησις

Opinion and conviction

In Athena’s teaching

When we turn to sensible objects we form opinions, beliefs and views, the 'my view and your view' prized in democracy, and she places them inside the cave, in what she calls the deep cave. They rest on the belief 'I am the body and others are bodies'. A conviction is an opinion clothed in emotion, which is why even science, studied only materialistically, can turn into dogma and fanaticism, as Kuhn saw with paradigms.

  • The separate self

    Changing a conviction threatens the knower's role.

The path

ἥρως / ἆθλος

The heroic path

hḗrōs / âthlos

In Athena’s teaching

In Athena's reading the hero is not a romantic figure but a stage in the evolution of consciousness, as Plato and later Platonism describe it. Human consciousness turns in the cycle of days; then suddenly something pushes, and a spark of eros lights, eros in the ontological sense: 'this does not fill me, I want my freedom'. From there begin the labours (ἆθλοι) needed to find who one is at one's centre, like Theseus going to the heart of the labyrinth. Ἥρως comes from ἔρως, so without eros there is no heroic path.

Another angle

Self-knowledge is a marathon that never stops, and Athena calls it athletics: ἀθλητισμός comes from ἆθλος. So every temple had a stadium or gymnasium beside it (at Delphi the stadium stands above the temple of Apollo, and the gymnasium near Athena Pronaia is larger than the temple), and the ancient schools began with the body: train the soul as you train the body. The hero must go against the currents of illusion set by upbringing, inner programming, fate (εἱμαρμένη) or society, with the strength (σθένος) of Athena, goddess of all heroes. After the ἆθλος comes the ἔπαθλον: completion, fullness, peace and love.

Athena connects it to

  • Eros

    Ἥρως comes from ἔρως: without eros there is no heroic path.

  • The sudden

    Suddenly something pushes and a spark of eros lights.

  • Athena (the goddess)

    Athena guides every hero: Theseus, Odysseus, Heracles.

  • Courageous nobility

    The hero needs the strength to go against the current.

  • Consciousness

    Plato treats the heroic as a stage of human consciousness.

  • The separate self

    Theseus must reach the centre of the labyrinth and kill the Minotaur, the ego.

  • Illusion and interpretation

    The hero goes against currents of illusion from upbringing, programming, fate or society.

  • Know thyself

    Self-knowledge is a marathon, an ἆθλος for a hero.

The good life

οἰκεῖον ἔργον / οἰκειοπραγία

One's own work

oikeîon érgon / oikeiopragía

In Athena’s teaching

To young people asking what to study and to adults whose fire has gone out, Athena gives the same answer: come to your centre, listen to your heart and ask what you love to do. The ancients held that every soul is born with a mission, its οἰκεῖον ἔργον, the work closest and warmest to its heart; doing what is one's own is οἰκειοπραγία. Fulfil it and you feel full and εὐδαίμων. Athena's two criteria: you burn with zeal for it, and while doing it you lose the sense of time, because love works in eternity.

Another angle

Athena calls those who have lost it σβηστοί, extinguished people: the flame of youth has gone out, swallowed by daily life, and they say their life does not fill them and they live as if imprisoned. To one who loves music but works as a marketing director Athena's advice is simple: become a musician. Follow love, and love will set you free.

    Do what you love: love shows each soul its own work.

  • Eudaimonia

    Fulfilling one's own work makes one full and εὐδαίμων.

  • Eternity and time

    In one's own work one loses the sense of time.

  • Freedom

    Follow love, and love will set you free.

  • The true Self

    To find it, come to your centre and listen to your heart.

Ways of knowing

πίστις

Faith (pistis)

pístis

In Athena’s teaching

For Athena faith is not the opposite of knowledge but a necessary step towards it, a 'scientific stage' found in the theory of knowledge of Plato's Republic: the interval between ignorance and knowledge. To believe (πιστεύω) is to give credit (πίστωση) that something may be so, as a scientist believes a new theory possible before shutting himself in the lab to prove it; that is why πίστη sits inside the word ἐπιστήμη. Faith in the good is the voice of Mnemosyne in us, an inner knowing that our nature, like the nature of the universe, is the Good.

Another angle

At the summit faith ends. In union, which Plotinus calls not a vision but a union, one no longer believes in God or the Good but is its witness and lives it. Because this goes beyond discursive knowing it cannot be put in terms of knowledge: there is the faith that leads, and its fruit, the experience itself.

Athena connects it to

  • Science and spirit

    Πίστη sits inside ἐπιστήμη: the scientist believes before proving.

  • Ignorance as separateness

    Faith is the interval between ignorance and knowledge.

  • Plato's Republic

    The Republic's theory of knowledge holds faith as a stage.

  • Recollection (anamnesis)

    Faith in the good is the voice of Mnemosyne within us.

  • The Good

    It believes because it already knows our nature is the Good.

  • Union with the Monad

    At union faith ends: you witness and live it.
